sample_q_texts: Cultured cells transplanted into immunocompromised recipients still present a significant risk of transmitting viruses that replicate in recipient tissues, posing a challenging challenge in tissue engineering. Recent studies have revealed that endocytosis, a fundamental cellular process that enhances antigen presentation and cross-presentation, can provide a framework for controlled viral delivery to ectopic tissues. However, little is known about the cellular and molecular mechanisms that promote organelle-based viral delivery, which necessitates the development of specific endocytic inhibitors to render viral replication and disease pathology within host tissues unfeasible. Here, we uncover cell-mediated endosomal antivirulence signaling as a mechanism that enables pathogens to enter and persist in endosomes within cell bodies. To demonstrate this, we discovered that the Adeno-Associated Virus Gamma (AAV) endogenous capsid remains intact in endosomes, even when the viral genome replicates in lysosomes. We further define the critical endocytic events that mediate viral delivery to the cell body, revealing that endosomal defenses that require high binding affinity response elements (ARPEGE domains) in Rab5 are exploited by virus-infected cells to reach the cell body and initiate continuous replication processes. We propose that the collective effects of this endocytic trafficking and molecular countermeasures contribute to the establishment of antiviral memory responses, which can promote successful maintenance of cell-based viral therapies.

Prolonged infections due to CoV-2 remain a major challenge for clinical scientists. In response, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) against several rhinoviruses have been generated by neutralizing anti-envelope mAbs such as sotrovimab and convalescent sera from COVID-recovered individuals. Recently, these mAbs have demonstrated their ability to inhibit several non-coding RNAs, which regulate various host and pathogen response pathways, including the innate immune response (IRT), stimulating an antiviral memory function. One of these RNAs, 70S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) has been shown to function as a cytomegalovirus (CMV) prime in both human and murine cells. However, the impact of the corresponding anti-70S mAbs on the mitochondrial antiviral signaling (MAS), one of the IRT sensors, has not yet been determined. Therefore, in the present study, we compared the antiviral activity and toxic effects of these antibodies against two diverse bat coronaviruses (Bat-CoV and Covid-19), two human rhinoviruses (FH-16, and A/MtF12), and one human cell line. Our results demonstrated that 5% anti-70S antibodies showed both remarkable antiviral activity and toxic effects on cells. Notably, 5% anti-70S antibodies also induced specific MAS in human cells, demonstrating their potential as potent IRTs. Furthermore, they reduced virus replication levels by approximately 30% in cell lines. Our findings uncover that 5% anti-70S antibodies stimulate both cell antiviral responses and pathogenesis, and reveal them as critical IRTs. As such, these results call for the reevaluation of the available antibodies, emphasizing the potential risks associated with suboptimal selection in antibody production.

Viruses are difficult to exploit for host immunity because they are generally less immunogenic than more advanced virus strains. Microglia, a highly active type of immune cells in the central nervous system (CNS) plays a role in combating viruses and other pathogens. However, the loss of immunogenic viruses from CNS remains elusive. Here, we show that an immunogenic virus, Moto, is largely lost in microglia from a brain explant where it was expressed. Interestingly, Moto-induced microglia were not the primary microglia, the neuronal cells differentiate into microglial cells whose population changed qualitatively. In contrast, Moto-induced cell line was the primary microglia. The severe phenotype and modified morphologies of Moto-induced microglia suggest that the loss of immunogenic viruses acts as a protective mechanism by inactivating pathogenic viruses while keeping host cells of motivirus-infected neurons to limit viral loads in these neurons and minimize neuron damage.

Polyoma viruses are intracellular bacteria capable of establishing persistent infection in their host. By utilizing single-pass sequencing technology, we designed novel codon composition for fully transcriptomic analysis that was capable of simultaneously profiling T cell and pathogen diversity, identifying candidate pathogen protein products. Based on this design, we identified candidate gene variations responsible for inefficient vaccine responses, viral replication, and costimulatory signaling. During early phase of infection, matrix protein (POL) and beta 1 galactosylation function were highly conserved between viruses and are associated with pathogenesis, antigen processing, and modulation of immune responses. This study challenges the traditional understanding of viral heterogeneity, provides a generalizable framework for detecting phenotypic differentiation, and paves the way for tailored genetic and personalized antiviral vaccination.

RSV1/GagA is key for the virion's endocytosis-to-exocytosis interaction and has been widely exploited to develop anti-RSV vaccine, but the virus load is difficult to visualize. Here, by confocal cell staining and live image reconstruction, we demonstrate a visible sensing device (bensonian condenser) for the dynamic visualization of virus loads inside cells. Mice exposed to RSV1/GagA-infected cells showed abundant virus inclusions in the endosomes and enhanced recombination efficiency in infected cells compared to controls. These results demonstrate the feasibility of a live cell monitoring system to visualize viruses and determine their molecular functions and potential infectivity. Furthermore, we propose that adding a rhP antigen can increase the susceptibility of recovered mice to new RSV1/GagA-infected cells. These findings advance vaccine research and provide strategies for assessing viral host defenses and predicting viral infectivity to improve its anti-RSV effect.

Red Blood Cells (RBCs) are essential in the prevention of pathogens and have been described as hot spots of certain infectious diseases. Prior research identified the placenta and near-to-birth origin as a potential source for carrying viral infections. However, little is understood of how viruses are incorporated during placental transfer and their effect on placental origin and subsequent fetus development. Using a unique Mendelian disease mouse model, we found a substantial in vivo reprogramming of the RBCs that allow viral vectors to enter and propagate throughout the placenta. We used a viral gene targeting strategy, termed viral load engineered (VLE), to co-opt the effect of a homologous molecular sequence for antiviral effects. Upon eradication of E. coli septicemia, we observed the induction of new viruses in the RBCs which could also be eradicated via VLE. Consequently, we conclude that a single episome represents a functional viral reservoir that facilitates the transition of fetal infection through human placentas with reduced or nullergic tolerance. Altogether, our findings imply that the highly-integrated placenta, RNA in the RBCs, and the maternally-derived viral load offer a novel potential escape route for perinatal pathogens to move from infected fetus to the baby's cord blood.

AMK10K (AMP-activated kinase K mouse ortholog) is a Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) that is mutated in multiple types of cancer and causes liver cancer cell death. Utilizing the Nobel Prize-winning Amheregene JrPMK10K-120-AMK10K retrovirus, we inactivated this ortholog in liver cancer cells from two African green monkey tumors, and observed a drastic improvement in tumor growth, despite the inability to observe gene expression changes. This is the first report of use of this engineered virus for therapeutic gene therapy. This protocol demonstrates the ability to develop highly efficient strategies for the production and delivery of engineered proteins.

Rapid decrease in resource availability during the COVID-19 pandemic led to mass production of SARS-CoV-2 antibody. In order to maintain antibody production during and beyond the pandemic, Duchenne muscle disease was transplanted to individuals who lost their muscles to contracture. This experiment is particularly relevant for the COVID-19 pandemic as Duchenne muscular dystrophy is the most prevalent genetic disease that can be transmitted from mother to offspring through the placenta, during pre- or post-natal period. We sought to explore whether non-dutchoulike, "store-and-release" versions of duchenne muscle transplants can be used in the post-pandemic era. Prior to testing this approach, we developed a long-term non-ddM long-term storage method that is based on a systematic, non-optimal replacement of diploid cells with diploid cells (substituted-PCR). The interplay between stress and the hepatitis C virus (HCV) envelope glycoprotein (E) is critical for liver infection and the immune response to chronic HCV infection. The Rab5A/Rab5B-interacting subunit c 34V is required for E-dependent signaling in hepatocytes and may also play a role in viral entry. In this study, we used six single-site mutations to create a single-site deficiency in Rab5A/Rab5B, Rab5A/pRab5A, and the Rab5/Rab5A/pRab5A asymmetric defect. Knocking out the Rab5A protein subunits in these c 34V-deficient systems had no effect on HCV replication, yet they significantly impaired the protective immune response that was observed when the HCV E was present. In HSV-1 and CMV, the data support the hypothesis that Rab5A provides a barrier against HVC activation, while Rab5 and Rab5B were critical for viral entry. The additional effect of Rab5A/pRab5A was unexpected and can be explained by the specific cellular context in which Rab5 and Rab5B are found. These data suggest that Rab5A can be particularly vulnerable to mutations, facilitating viral entry in the absence of the antiviral defense, opening an opportunity for enhancing these neutralizing properties.

A disturbance in the immune response to pathogens leading to an inflammation state has long been regarded as the basis for the development of chronic viral disease. Using genetic mutation analysis, we show that this model is not sufficient to explain the development of the chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) and the chronic non-lymphocytic leukaemia (CML) malignancies. By combining immunofluorescence and quantitative viral plaque assay, we demonstrate that a L8101 defect in the TIGIT viral receptor of the Z23.0 clone of human adenoviruses promotes lymphoid leukaemia formation. We find that the L8101 mutation in TIGIT alone is sufficient for neoplastic transformation, while, in combination with viral sRNA-mediated transcriptional suppression and inducible activation of T cell memory, the L8101 mutation synergizes with this effect. These results indicate that dysregulation of the regulatory network between self-T-cell TIGIT and the extracellular pathogen-derived RNA modulates the formation of chronic viral leukaemia.
sample_p_texts: Fever during influenza A virus (IAV) infection is triggered by the innate immune response. Various factors contribute to this response, including IAV mini viral RNAs (mvRNA), which trigger RIG-I signaling when their replication and transcription are dysregulated by template loops (t-loop). While fever is a symptom of the infection, it also alters the environment in which virus replicates. This changing environment may impact the viral infection cycle and in turn disease outcome. Here we show that IAV infection at temperatures that simulate fever leads to increased mvRNA synthesis and antiviral signaling. Mathematical modeling and experimental analyses reveal that differential IAV nucleoprotein and RNA polymerase production underlies the increased mvRNA level. Moreover, at the higher infection temperature mvRNAs with dysregulating t-loops contribute most to the innate immune activation. We propose that fever-enhanced mvRNA production is a self-amplifying feedback loop that may affect infection outcome.

Adeno-associated virus (AAV) has found immense success as a delivery system for gene therapy, yet the small 4.7 kb packaging capacity of the AAV sharply limits the scope of its application. In addition, high doses of AAV are frequently required to facilitate therapeutic effects, leading to acute toxicity issues. While dual and triple AAV approaches have been developed to mitigate the packaging capacity problem, these necessitate even higher doses to ensure that co-infection occurs at sufficient frequency. To address these challenges, we herein describe a novel delivery system consisting of adenovirus (Ad) covalently linked to multiple adeno-associated virus (AAV) capsids as a new way of more efficiently co-infecting cells with lower overall amounts of AAVs. We utilize the DogTag-DogCatcher (DgT-DgC) molecular glue system to construct our AdAAVs and we demonstrate that these hybrid virus complexes achieve enhanced co-transduction of cultured cells, including primary cells. This technology may eventually broaden the utility of AAV gene delivery by providing an alternative to dual or triple AAV which can be employed at lower dose while reaching higher co-transduction efficiency.

High pathogenicity avian influenza viruses pose a growing threat to poultry, livestock, wildlife, and humans as they undergo accelerated expansion of host and geographical ranges. Since 2020, these viruses have driven a panzootic characterized by extensive viral diversification and spillover into species previously considered to be resistant to the disease. There is currently a lack of physiologically relevant in vitro models that can be used to screen the rapidly changing viral landscape. To address this need, we describe the first chicken lung organoids derived from adult stem cells of specific pathogen free White Leghorns. We analyze their gene expression with bulk RNA sequencing, confirm their cellular heterogeneity via single-nuclei RNA sequencing, and provide basic morphological characterization using hematoxylin and eosin staining, immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence, and transmission electron microscopy. The results indicate that the organoids contained several cell types, including non-ciliated columnar, cuboidal, squamous, and mucin-producing cells, representative of different regions of the avian respiratory system. Furthermore, expression of genes relevant to influenza A virus infection and replication appeared to be conserved across different sample types. These organoids have the potential to effectively and efficiently model viral infection of the chicken lung, enabling the investigation of viral pathogenesis and evolutionary potential, virus-host interactions, and discovery of targets for antiviral treatments.

Plaque assays are typically quantified at an endpoint and fail to capture the temporal dynamics of viral infection and spread. In this study we introduce a high-throughput method utilising live-cell imaging and a recombinant vaccinia virus (VACV) engineered to express two fluorescent transgenes linked to distinct replication phases. This novel approach allows for real-time tracking of VACV plaques from their inception at a single infected cell through to multicellular expansion, enabling detailed kinetic analysis of plaque development. Using this analysis pipeline we categorise VACV plaque formation into three distinct phases: Establishment, Expansion, and Exhaustion, and quantitatively describe their dynamics. Our findings reveal significant variability in the initiation time of plaque spread (from single-cell to multicellular stages) and the growth rate of plaques, both between individual plaques and across different cell lines. This variability underscores the influence of host cellular factors on the kinetics of viral replication. Additionally, we reveal that the viral replication cycle dramatically accelerates through the early phases of plaque formation, which we hypothesise is driven by the changing multiplicity of cellular infection at the plaque edge. Finally, we demonstrate that differences in plaque sizes between two cell lines (BS-C-1 and HaCaT) can be largely attributed to variations in viral replication rate. This research reinforces the value of live-cell fluorescence microscopy in elucidating the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of viral infections, and contributes to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms driving viral spread and replication kinetics.

The Rous sarcoma virus (RSV) is an onco-retrovirus that infects avian species such as the chicken (Gallus gallus). RSV is the first oncovirus to be described and the oncogenic activity of this virus is related to the expression of a tyrosine kinase that induces carcinogenic transformation. Interestingly, we have noted that the RSV genome contains various potential G4 forming sequences. Among these, two sequences located in the GAG and POL genes, respectively, show high G4 forming potential. Additionally, the SRC oncogene also harbours a putative G4 forming sequence. In this study, we have characterised the G4 formation and topology in these three loci in the RSV-DNA. We have found that these sequences form dynamic G4 structures in physiological conditions and such dynamicity may be associated with their cellular functions. Further, we have also established that these G4s are recognized by G4 interacting small-molecule ligands and the G4-stabilizing protein nucleolin. Binding of these ligands induces structural shifts in the G4 leading to change in structure and stability. Thus, the RSV-DNA G4s may be further studied as targets to control its infection and oncogenic effects.

We recently identified the FACT-ETS-1 Antiviral Response (FEAR) pathway as an interferon-independent innate immune response that restricts DNA virus replication and is countered by poxvirus-encoded A51R proteins (Rex et al., 2024, Nature Microbiology). The human FEAR pathway is mediated by the FACT complex, consisting of hSpt16 and SSRP1 subunits, that remodels chromatin to activate expression of the antiviral transcription factor, ETS-1. To counter this pathway, poxvirus A51R proteins tether SUMOylated hSpt16 subunits to microtubules to prevent ETS-1 expression. While these observations indicate a role for the FEAR pathway in DNA virus restriction, it was unclear if RNA viruses interact with this pathway. Here, we show that RNA viruses are also restricted by the FEAR pathway, yet encode mechanisms distinct from poxviruses to counter this response. We show vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), a rhabdovirus, utilizes its matrix (M) protein to promote proteasome-dependent degradation of SUMOylated hSpt16 and to block ETS-1 nuclear import. Strains encoding mutant M proteins that cannot antagonize the FEAR pathway exhibit replication defects in human cells that can be rescued by hSpt16 or ETS-1 depletion. Moreover, FACT inhibitor treatment enhanced the replication of oncolytic VSV strains encoding defective M proteins in restrictive cancer cells, suggesting FEAR pathway inhibition may improve oncolytic virotherapy. Strikingly, we provide evidence that the inability of VSV M to degrade SUMOylated Spt16 in lepidopteran insect cells results in abortive infection, suggesting VSV-Spt16 interactions influence virus host range. Lastly, we show that human and murine paramyxovirus target SUMOylated Spt16 proteins for degradation in human and murine cells utilizing a conserved N-terminal motif in their accessory "C" proteins. Collectively, our study illustrates that DNA and RNA viruses have independently evolved diverse mechanisms to antagonize SUMOylated host Spt16 proteins, underscoring the physiological importance of the FEAR pathway to antiviral immunity.

Coronaviruses (CoV) emerge suddenly from animal reservoirs to cause novel diseases in new hosts. Discovered in 2012, Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) is endemic in camels in the Middle East and is continually causing local outbreaks and epidemics. While all three newly emerging human CoV from past 20 years (SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV) cause respiratory disease, each CoV has unique host interactions that drive differential pathogeneses. To better understand the virus and host interactions driving lethal MERS-CoV infection, we performed a longitudinal multi-omics analysis of sublethal and lethal MERS-CoV infection in mice. Significant differences were observed in body weight loss, virus titers and acute lung injury among lethal and sub-lethal virus doses. Virus induced apoptosis of type I and II alveolar epithelial cells suggest that loss or dysregulation of these key cell populations was a major driver of severe disease. Omics analysis suggested differential pathogenesis was multi-factorial with clear differences among innate and adaptive immune pathways as well as those that regulate lung epithelial homeostasis. Infection of mice lacking functional T and B-cells showed that adaptive immunity was important in controlling viral replication but also increased pathogenesis. In summary, we provide a high-resolution host response atlas for MERS-CoV infection and disease severity. Multi-omics studies of viral pathogenesis offer a unique opportunity to not only better understand the molecular mechanisms of disease but also to identify genes and pathways that can be exploited for therapeutic intervention all of which is important for our future pandemic preparedness.

ImportanceEmerging coronaviruses like SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV cause a range of disease outcomes in humans from asymptomatic, moderate and severe respiratory disease which can progress to death but the factors causing these disparate outcomes remain unclear. Understanding host responses to mild and life-threatening infection provides insight into virus-host networks within and across organ systems that contribute to disease outcomes. We used multi-omics approaches to comprehensively define the host response to moderate and severe MERS-CoV infection. Severe respiratory disease was associated with dysregulation of the immune response. Key lung epithelial cell populations that are essential for lung function get infected and die. Mice lacking key immune cell populations experienced greater virus replication but decreased disease severity implicating the immune system in both protective and pathogenic roles in the response to MERS-CoV. These data could be utilized to design new therapeutic strategies targeting specific pathways that contribute to severe disease.

SUMO-modified Tripartite Motif Protein 28 (TRIM28; KAP1) plays a crucial role in repressing endogenous retroelement (ERE) transcription. We previously provided evidence that loss of SUMO-modified TRIM28 triggered by influenza A virus (IAV) infection promotes activation of host antiviral immunity via a mechanism involving derepression of EREs and production of immunostimulatory RNAs. While the IAV NS1 protein might limit consequences of such activation via its dsRNA-binding activity, we hypothesized that other human pathogenic viruses could have evolved more direct strategies to counteract this potential ERE-based defense system. Here, we reveal that V proteins from diverse paramyxoviruses, including Measles, Mumps, Parainfluenza, and Nipah/Hendra viruses, can all engage with TRIM28. Notably, the efficiency of engagement varies markedly between virus species, a phenotype that can be linked to specific residues within the C-terminal domain of V proteins. Further mapping showed that V proteins target both the TRIM28 Coiled-Coil domain and the TRIM28 PHD-Bromodomain, which contains the functionally-relevant TRIM28 SUMO-modification sites necessary for ERE repression. In this context, while paramyxovirus infection triggers canonical stress-associated phosphorylation of TRIM28, loss of SUMO-modified TRIM28 does not occur, and minimal induction of the TRIM28-dependent ERE RNA, HERVK14C, is observed. Furthermore, pre-infection with Parainfluenza virus type 2, which encodes a V protein that efficiently engages with TRIM28, limits subsequent IAV-triggered loss of SUMO-modified TRIM28 and upregulation of HERVK14C RNA. These findings dissect the interplay between paramyxoviruses and TRIM28, providing support for the concept of a TRIM28-regulated ERE-based antiviral defense system by uncovering a potential viral antagonistic measure.

ImportanceHost recognition of viral nucleic acids is fundamental for stimulating antiviral immunity. To prevent aberrant immune activation, cells must precisely differentiate "non-self" from "self" nucleic acids. Endogenous retroelements (EREs), despite their self-origin, can produce immunostimulatory RNAs that blur this distinction, and may have been functionally co-opted to enhance antiviral immunity in response to some infections. Normally, ERE transcription is repressed by the host protein TRIM28, the function of which is dynamically modulated by SUMO-modification. Here, we demonstrate that paramyxoviruses engage TRIM28, maintaining it in its repressive, SUMO-modified form during infection. We propose that this virus-host interaction limits ERE activation and consequently suppresses ERE-driven immune signaling, revealing a previously unidentified mechanism of immune evasion by paramyxoviruses.

As well as spreading through virions, influenza A viruses (IAVs) can evade antiviral drugs and neutralising antibodies by spreading directly from cell to cell. In cell culture this can occur by the induction of intercellular membrane connections known as tunnelling nanotube-like structures (TLSs), which are capable of trafficking the viral genome between cells. Here, we showed that TLSs are present at the site of IAV infections in vivo, and then used in vitro models to ask how IAVs induce their formation. We found that TLS induction cannot be induced by cytokine signalling from infected to uninfected cells, but requires IAV replication within cells. IAV replication can form filamentous virions with structural similarities to TLSs, but we found that TLS induction is independent of virion morphology. We therefore looked at the intracellular responses to infection. Using a pan-caspase inhibitor, we found that TLS induction by IAVs requires the onset of apoptosis. Our results, which suggest that IAVs control their ability to spread directly from cell to cell by driving infected cells into apoptosis, identifies a new way in which a virus can manipulate its host to evade antiviral immune responses.

Author SummaryInfluenza A viruses (IAVs) spread efficiently through the respiratory tract in the form of extracellular virus particles, but can be restricted by neutralising antibodies and antiviral drugs. IAVs can avoid this restriction by transporting viral genomes directly from one cell to the next. They can do this by inducing the formation of long, thin intercellular connections known as tunnelling nanotube-like structures, which are capable of trafficking viral genomes. In this study, we demonstrate for the first time that tunnelling-nanotube like structures form within IAV infected lungs. We then asked how IAVs induce these structures. We found that cell death pathways triggered by IAV replication induce the formation of tunnelling nanotube-like structures, thereby establishing routes of infection spread to other cells. In this way, the virus exploits the cell death response of its host to ensure that its infection can continue to spread even within the restrictive environment of the respiratory tract.

Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is a leading pathogen causing acute viral hepatitis globally. While HEV is primarily spread fecal-orally, the role of the gut in HEV pathogenesis remains largely unexplored, including how HEV disseminates from gut to liver, and whether the gut is an HEV reservoir. We here aimed to illuminate HEV biology in the gut using human intestinal enteroids (HIEs).

Three strategies were explored to establish an HEV-HIE model: three-dimensional (3D) HIEs, two-dimensional (2D) HIEs in transwell, and HEV RNA-electroporated HIEs. HEV particles produced by electroporated HIEs were characterized by western blot and gradient centrifugation. The intestinal tropism of HEV was investigated through confocal fluorescent microscopy and gene expression analysis.

HEV infection in 3D-HIEs and 2D-HIEs showed limited replication, whereas HIEs electroporation led to a sustained increase in the release of non-enveloped infectious virions. These virions could re-infect new 3D-HIEs, yielding a [~]2 log10 increase in HEV RNA. In electroporated HIEs, high expression of the infectious ORF2 capsid form was observed in the supernatant. Importantly, 70% of all HEV-infected cells were identified as proliferative cells. ORF2 staining was also observed in absorptive enterocytes, goblet, and enteroendocrine cells.

Overall, we established a robust HEV-HIE model that yields high titers of infectious non-enveloped virions. Proliferative cells and the fast intestinal epithelial cell turnover are important features that facilitate efficient HEV replication, and likely also its dissemination. This study suggests that the gut is an HEV reservoir, capable of producing some of the non-enveloped HEV shed in the feces.

SignificanceHepatitis E virus (HEV) causes [~]20 million enterically transmitted cases of viral hepatitis globally. To better understand the largely unexplored role of the gut during an HEV infection, we used human intestinal enteroids (HIEs). We show that HEV-electroporated HIEs produce highly infectious non-envelopedHEV particles, resulting in a more efficient re-infection compared with traditional gold-standard methods. Importantly, we detected HEV in multiple human intestinal epithelial cell types within the human intestinal epithelium, with the majority of proliferative cells infected. This model offers valuable insights into the intestinal tropism of HEV and can serve to further investigate chronic HEV infection in the gut. Moreover, this underscores the importance of using physiologically relevant models to unravel details of HEV infection in the gut.

sample_q_texts: Stomatitis is a devastating disease of cattle, and similar management practices are inadequate to prevent or treat the disease. To achieve significant reductions in cattle mastitis, optimization of cattle hygiene practices and effective vaccines must be coupled with the application of multiple integrated husbandry strategies. As part of this approach, prophylactic high oleic (HOOL) triglyceride meal (TM) inclusion into the diet of cattle is used. To study optimal inclusion levels of HOOL within diet, a stepwise degradation of dietary requirements was evaluated. Aiming for more digestible dietary fibre to improve animal performance, availability of more rumen microbial mass would provide CO2 or CO2 equivalent reduction. Six types of diet were fed to cattle: an arm containing 2% HOOL, 10% (MA), 20% (II) and 30% (IV) to 60% (VL) free-choice feed, 5% (AI) and 80% (VL) pre-mixed mix, 5% (DRD) and 90% (ML) home-block diet, 1% (DRD) home-block meal and an unfortified maize mix. These four test diets varied in total TEF, dry matter (DM) and fatty acid profiles between each other, but differences were less pronounced than a straight forward reformulation of rations. The MA result from 0% HOOL TEF in three different trial designs, with DM percentages of 100, 70 and 53%, and DM values ranging between 20% and 32% in the mix-fed trials (HLD). HOOL TEF inclusion levels of 10% or 30% was required in all other diets to achieve utilisation of rumen-mediated NO digestion of dietary fibre. Post-holistic is typical of diet where the inclusion of 10% of HOOL food is recognised as insufficient. Using the Hull-Spill, residue, and production ratio (HSPR), 10% HOOL was used in the MA trial, resulting in a substantial (6.20%) increase in crude protein (CP) and energy, and a decrease in DMI ratio. This illustrates that the benefits of HOOL selection outweigh the costs of production and trade-off between nutrients, and remains ideal for cattle in the clinical trial.

Plagues caused by obligate intracellular parasites severely challenge the health of native vertebrate populations, with both hosts and pathogens perpetuating infection within their body. In the mammalian intestine, these parasites aggregate and interfere with intestinal homeostatic processes. Here we study a novel IAT1/IAT1-like protein named DL3071, that exists as a unique, naturally found, and at least partially protected, multiple host immunogenic protein (MHIP). D2807, a structural variant of the core IAT1 protein, infects intestinal crypts, and its selective expression in IAT1 mutants leads to impaired intestinal barrier integrity and severity of enteric symptoms. We conducted chemical proteomics screen experiments to identify a molecule encoded by DL3071 and demonstrate a putative IAT1 function within the epithelial membrane. First, we report that DL3071 binds to its target, the double-helical transmembrane nucleoporin AP10, with minimal residue flexibility at the CB66 site, where the coiled-coil domain and stretch also mediate binding. Second, we demonstrate that DL3071 activates bacterial colicins from Clostridium difficile, genetically fused to an IAT1 extracellular domain. Lastly, we demonstrate that DL3071 binding to AP10 selectively activates selected bacterial virulence factors. Collectively, we show that DL3071 likely requires additional interactions for selective modulation of bacterial gut bacteria, and we present potential therapeutic candidates.

PurposeThe development of non-invasive testing methods for rapid diagnosis of COVID-19 or the advent of a rapid test for COVID-19 stand against current standard non-invasive diagnostic methods. The high cost associated with acquiring the developed test may lead to its inaccessibility and limited availability in the country. In this study, we assessed the potential of low-cost and easily available probiotic-enriched milk for production of COVID-19 diagnostic probiotic oligosaccharide. Methods A CRISPR/Cas9-based primer-primer analysis with a specific screening for R281Q Probiotic Lactococcus plantarum (LP1405) was carried out to identify genome of L. plantarum/LP1405, and the colony morphology of the colony was assessed to identify unique motif of L. plantarum. Based on the biofilm assay, our results demonstrated growth inhibition of MDA-MB231 when challenged with virus and further PLA2 treatment which partially inhibited the growth. Dose-dependent experimental results demonstrated that isolated probiotic oligosaccharide (PLOS) dissolved at a 0.05 M concentration (0.04 mL/10mL), had greater inhibition rate of the TLYZ-T virus than the other three virus strains. In contrast, a lysate with 0.08 M concentration (0.4 mL) of PLOS did not inhibit COVID-19 in whole form, but it had a less inhibitory effect on the virus. Some differences were observed in the growth and membrane integrity of the results between the controls and the immobilized virus. Finally, the fact that PLOS has highly enhanced effects on the inhibition of LDV-1 and L. azithraeicphylum strains showed that it is effectively beneficial to the TLYZ-T and L. azithraeicphylum strains. Confirmed by cell death and adhesion assays. Conclusion The probiotic probiotic oligosaccharide of L. plantarum (LP1405) was successfully developed through this study.

The gut microbiome is essential for the maintenance of intestinal homeostasis. In healthy individuals, the gut microbiota (HM) exhibits high variability from person to person. Several diet-dependent genomic disorders, such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), are primarily caused by eating habits transmitted through the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) and likely involving intestinal bacteria. However, the impact of gut bacteria on the gut microbiota and liver organs in maintaining the gut microbiota is unknown. In this study, our data show that the consumption of a probiotic culture containing unidentified bacteria rich in bacterial protein hydrolysis and fine particulate matter (up to 31 mg/kg), supplemented with enteric Bacteroides for 34 days, led to increased Firmicutes and attenuated Akkermansia-related diseases. We propose that these changes in the gut microbiota lead to the activation of Toll-like receptor 7 mediated immunity, which removes mucus, mucus-rich pathogens, and promotes the release of antimicrobial peptides. These studies suggest that intestinal bacteria have the potential to regulate the gut microbiota and liver organs of healthy individuals and may have potential therapeutic benefits in inflammatory diseases involving the gut microbiota.

Current foodborne outbreaks involve hundreds to thousands of foodborne pathogens. Without public and specialized healthcare workers, detection and rapid isolation of pathogens are not feasible. Techniques such as liquid chromatography, inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LC-ICP-MS), flow-through mass spectrometry (LC-ICMS), and single-cell genomics (SC-MetG/MetO) have been successfully applied to meet these needs in a public health laboratory. The FDA-mandated US Food Quality Protection Act and the European (EU) Food Safety Authority harmonized methods within the Foodborne Pathogens Origin and Transmission (FPT) method for detecting foodborne pathogens and their proteomic features. To meet regulatory requirements of the EU, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), this method needs to be optimized towards one-minute chromatographic run times, and parallel media (e.g. PBS) for high-throughput LC-ICP-MS. The validation samples used in this new approach were the EU-standardized negative standards for the finger-prick test 432. The presence of 2.5 mg/ml of FPT-active compounds used in the negative standard gave a signal absorbance at 280 nm of 31 to 35 ?m. The method demonstrated a sensitivity and selectivity limit of 4 fg ml, a LOD of 2 ?g ml, and a precision of 1.3 and 2.3 % for FV-Cu/CuF (unitless: 5 15 ; 5 ?g/L), corresponding to a quantitative detection limit of 0.005 fg ml for TC. The method is compatible with several analytical columns with wide applications in food-testing labs. This method is an easy and rapid alternative to the standard test strips. In addition, in view of the ongoing pandemic COVID-19, this novel approach to food safety testing for genetically modified organisms (GMOs), could not only be applied immediately but also used to verify GMO products in the same way. In light of the above developments, here we present the method itself in the kind of analysis of the peptide OM655, an active compound of the PR4 cell line. The present work could contribute to the development of appropriate protocols for food-based analytical testing.

A study of microbial colonizations associated with dental calculus suggest a potential role for bacterial metabolism, particularly extracellular digestion, in ensuring blood supply to dental soft tissue surfaces. The goal of the study was to investigate the potential interactions between dental calculus, dental bacteria, and the oral cavity. This study used a clinical approach involving a clinician collecting calculus for histological analysis. The analysis focused on the mechanism of cross-contamination and bacterial contamination from dental calculus within the oral cavity. Bacterial analysis, using a multiplex PCR approach, included blood infection and the metabolic potential of dental calculus. The results from the study were outlined in a detailed photo graphic report. Additionally, histological and microbiological analysis was incorporated.

In the context of the United States Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), refugees and others may be prohibited from entry into the United States upon arrival due to limited resources. We developed 3 approaches to address the limited capacity of current medical and nutritional capacity to process and provide nutrition to non-citizen refugees and other travel bans. The first approach consists of a 3-d bioreactor (BMPC) that directly supplies food to insects in an encapsulated pouch with 600 cubic millimeters of solution. This approach extends both food and nutrient capacity when consumed directly by the insect by 74%. The second approach is a fully formed insect meal within a nutritive, matrix. This approach increases the quantity of food, fat, and protein with 667mg of protein and 927 mg of proteins contained within the meal. We assess nutrient digestibility of the protein in insect larvae within the entire, meal. We demonstrate that the soluble carotenoid fingerprint of the meal is present and in some cases, even at higher concentrations than what is observed for carotenoids isolated from a cell-free extract. The third approach is an insect gut microbiome solution. A 3D printed medium within a pouch provides the essential amino acids and peptides and vitamin requirements needed to support nutrient-responsive gut microbes and commensal microbes. These approaches have the potential to expand the supply of nutrition for non-citizen refugees who may not be able to cross the U.S. Line, making access to imported foods an issue in the United States.

Author SummaryResearch in the fields of food immunology, nutrition, and medicine is trying to identify food products and substances that can be consumed by refugees who have been excluded from entering the United States due to medical or biosecurity limitations. In the case of the United States, refugees are those who come from countries where the United States, not being able to afford these goods, has limited to no resources to provide these items to these individuals. More recently there have been concerns that the limited biosecurity measures being used in the US due to Covid-19 have resulted in the inability of many refugees to enter the country and the system to take their place.

Duodenal diseases affect the integrity of the small intestine through a malfunction of its intestinal epithelium, leading to nutrient loss and metabolic disorders. Antibiotics act on various microbial species and have been shown to affect various gut disorders. Yet, the interactions and consequences of different antibiotics on the gut flora are still not fully understood. To uncover those interactions, we applied a complex metaproteomic approach and conducted proteomics-based transcriptomic studies on fecal samples from six patients affected with non-obstructive reflux disease (NERD), bacterial-related Crohn disease (BRCD), gastric adenocarcinoma (GA) patients and healthy controls (HC). For proteomic analysis, 3566 clean and well-isolated samples were evaluated using chemiluminescent protein arrays (ClPA) from LC-MS to identify bacterial and bacterial-associated proteins (BAPs) against the multiclass-matched clinical sample used in this study, which included 5565 proteins for analysis. In contrast to BAPs, a functional protein taxonomy identified only 546 out of the 5500 likely protein candidates that overlapped with the original clinical samples. Seven proinflammatory species of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Bacillus subtilis and Streptococcus agalactiae were detected in the fecal samples; therefore, the ClPA model selected species belonged to these genera. Among other species, Klebsiella pneumoniae was commonly identified in the bacterial-associated proteins group and was found to be related to respiratory disease, digestive system diseases, skin diseases, anti-infectious bacteria and inflammation. In summary, this study's conclusions suggest the diverse species of bacteria found in the gut flora play a major role in the influence of antibiotic treatment in medical conditions, which may explain the different clinical symptoms caused by antibiotic treatment.

The human gizzard (digestive tract) is an understudied, isolated structure that directly interacts with the human gastrointestinal tract and absorbs food molecules. Despite this direct physical contact, evidence of the mammalian digestive microbiota diversity in the gut, which can significantly modulate human health, is scarce. Using a novel host-guest, gizzard gizzard-derived microbiota isolated using metagenomic sequencing to investigate the potential microbiome impact of aberrant human feeding, a novel human-gizzard faba bean symbiosis was established on gizzard digestion in adult subjects. The group-level microbiome was revealed through strain-level phylogeny and determined the contribution of each subject to local symbiont communities, revealed by microbiome profiles, bacterial abundance, and microbiome diversity at the experimental length scale. Functional enrichment at the single-cell level revealed that the gizzard-digestive microbiota prioritized energy and carbohydrate digestion, both of which depend on harsh proteases produced and secreted by human digestive enzymes. Pathogenicity was determined using the antibiotic potency test, where the presence of a cloned human pathogen served as the antibiotic antibiotic antagonist, whereas the presence of a cloned plant pathogen served as an antibiotic antibiotic enhancer. Results from this study revealed that dietary faba bean consumption can promote local symbiont co-evolution of commensal microbiota within the mammalian gut, which explains human susceptibility to intestinal pathogens and the association between gizzard microbiota variations and pathobiont bacteria-drug virulence. Future study aims to link specific microbial reactions to human health and disease.

Human Gizzard-derived microbiota from adult volunteers (n=38) were enriched in foods as diverse as peanuts, legumes, berries, gizzard, fruits, onions, and processed food analogs, and displayed alterations in microbial diversity and abundance, composition and function, and bacterial pathogenicity. Based on their narrow foraging spectrum, we argue that individual dietary choices have negligible impact on intestinal symbiont diversity.

Probiotics are live microorganisms that supplement the microbial populations of the intestinal tract and affect human health. Probiotic bacterial strains possess many modes of action that influence the gut environment and other organisms and many species utilize specific mechanisms for employing probiotics to protect against parasites that are the main causes of food-borne illness and diarrhea in humans. This study aimed to investigate the role of several of these mechanisms at the bacterial-intestinal microbiome interface in relation to antimicrobial resistance and associated probiotic strains. In this study, we investigated probiotic strains in relationship to potential key mechanisms within the Intestinal Microbiota Boundary (IMB) in relation to ampicillin-resistant and ampicillin-resistant (AMP) sensitive strains. Using High-Resolution Mass Spectrometry (HRMS) coupled with structural proteomics, we quantified the proteolytic and cellular proteomic profiles of probiotic strains under dynamic stimulatory conditions (stimulation, low cell density, and low cell population) and compared them with the dynamic inhibitor conditions (high cell density, low cell population, and high cell density combined with inhibition).
sample_p_texts: Hydrogen sulfide is a gaseous, reactive molecule specifically enriched in the gastrointestinal tract. Here, we uncover a non-redundant role for sulfide in the control of both microbial and immune homeostasis of the gut. Notably, depletion of sulfide via both pharmaceutical and dietary interventions led to a profound collapse of CD4 T cells in the ileum of the small intestine lamina propria and significant impact on microbial ecology. As a result, mice with reduced sulfide within the gut were deficient in their ability to mount T cell dependent antibody responses to oral vaccine. Mechanistically, our results support the idea that sulfide could act directly on CD4 T cells via enhanced AP-1 activation, leading to heightened proliferation and cytokine production. This study uncovers sulfides as keystone components in gut ecology and provides mechanistic insight between diet, gut sulfide production and mucosal immunity.

IntroductionIngestion of nanomaterials (NMs) might impair intestinal barrier, but the underlying mechanisms remain evasive, and evidence is not systematically gathered or produced. A mechanistic-based approach would be instrumental to assess if relevant NMs disrupt intestinal barrier to support NM risk assessment in the food sector.

MethodsHere, we developed an adverse outcome pathway (AOP) based on biological plausibility and by leveraging existing information of an existing NM relevant AOP leading to hepatic outcomes. We then extracted the current evidence existing in the literature for a targeted selection of NMs with high food sector relevance, namely ZnO, CuO, FeO, SiO2, Ag NMs and nanocellulose.

ResultsWe propose a new AOP (AOP530) that starts with endocytic lysosomal uptake leading to lysosomal disruption inducing mitochondrial dysfunction. Mitochondrial impairments can lead to cell injury/death and disrupt the intestinal barrier. The evidence collected supports that those food NMs can be taken up by intestinal cells and indicates that intestinal barrier disruption by Ag, CuO, SiO2 NMs might occur whilst only few studies support that outcome for FeO, ZnO. Lysosomal disruption and mitochondrial dysfunction are rarely evaluated. For nanocellulose, none of the studies report toxic-related events.

ConclusionsCollecting the existing scientific evidence supporting our AOP linking NM uptake to intestinal barrier impairments allowed us to highlight current evidence gaps but also data inconsistencies. Those latter could be associated with the variety of stressors, biological systems and KE-related assays used in the different studies, calling for further harmonized methodologies and production of mechanistic evidence in the safety regulatory assessment of NMs in the food sector.

Saliva influences the release of aroma in the oral cavity. The composition of human saliva varies depending on stimulation and hosts origin; however, the compositional differences of saliva and their influences on aroma release have not been fully evaluated. In this study, we recruited 30 healthy adults (15 Australians and 15 Chinese) and collected saliva samples at three stages: before, during, and after stimulation. Salivary samples were characterised by flow rate, total protein concentration, esterase activity, microbiome composition by full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and the ability to release aroma from wine by headspace solid-phase microextraction gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (HS-SPME-GC-MS). Differences in salivary composition and specific wine volatiles were found between Australian and Chinese participants, and amongst the three stimulation stages. Significant correlations between the relative abundance of 3 bacterial species and 10 wine volatiles were observed. Our results confirm the influence of participants geographic origin and stimulation on salivary composition, highlighting the role of salivary components, especially salivary bacteria, on the release of aroma from wine.

The epithelium of the human gastrointestinal tract is key for controlling the absorption of small molecules and for forming a tight barrier between the gut microbiota and the host, thereby maintaining metabolic homeostasis. Both the microbiota and the barrier function of the intestinal epithelium have a role in pharmacokinetic variability of medical drugs. In this study, we developed a high-throughput workflow to assess the absorption of bacterially produced (drug) metabolites by intestinal epithelial cells through the combination of anaerobic bacterial cultures and human-intestine derived Caco2 cell cultures in a transwell system. To functionally monitor the barrier integrity during the experiments, we introduced a panel of marker compounds, whose concentration kinetics on either side of the epithelial monolayer indicates barrier integrity and transport. We employed this workflow to systematically probe the effect of different gut bacterial species on the epithelial absorption of 482 drugs and their 172 bacterially produced metabolites. While we could recapitulate known bacterial drug biotransformation reactions and expected drug metabolite absorption profiles, we also identified 33 new bacteria-drug pairs for which bacterial biotransformation alters epithelial permeability. Further, we combined the developed experimental workflow with untargeted metabolomics analysis to systematically study epithelial permeability of metabolites naturally produced by gut bacteria. Tracking the absorption kinetics of 397 bacterially produced metabolites revealed that the majority (>79%) of these metabolites do not pass the Caco2 monolayer, illustrating its role as a physical and metabolic barrier. In summary, we present a highly adaptable high-throughput workflow to quantitatively study the metabolic interactions at the intestinal microbiota-host interface which can impact pharmacokinetics, toxicokinetics, and human physiology.

Recent work suggests an altered duodenal mucosa-associated microbiota (MAM) in patients with functional dyspepsia (FD) when compared to outpatient controls, these differences may reflect alterations in host-microbiome homeostasis. Given that specific mucosal immune signatures have been identified in FD, we hypothesised that these changes would be associated with specific microbial changes. We aimed to profile the duodenal MAM to identify microbes associated with known changes in FD mucosal and peripheral immune homeostasis. Duodenal biopsies were collected from 11 asymptomatic outpatient controls and 17 FD patients. Separate biopsies were collected for MAM 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, histological evaluation, and mucosal lamina propria mononuclear cell (LPMC) isolation. Where available peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) were isolated from whole blood. PBMC and LPMC populations were analysed for CD4 and CD8 T cell populations by flow cytometry. Initial comparisons of histological and immune measures revealed significant differences between FD and outpatient controls, with decreased villi goblet cells and increased LPMC CD4 Central Memory, LPMC CD8, and PBMC CD4+ Central Memory Th17 in FD compared to controls. While microbiome profiles varied between groups, specific associations with the histological and immunological scoring found that in controls, villi goblet cells correlated positively with Massilia and negatively with Exiguobacterium, while FD patients showed no significant correlations. Additionally, controls exhibited a negative correlation between LPMC CD4 Central Memory and Veillonella, with FD patients showing no significant correlation. Notably, FD patients demonstrated a significant negative correlation between LPMC CD8 and Sulfophobococcus, and a positive correlation between PBMC CD4+ Central Memory Th17 and both Gemella and Fusobacterium.

ImportanceWhile several papers have reported the alteration in FD duodenal MAM, study numbers are low and consensus on specific biomarker signatures within the microbiome have not been reached. Our findings contribute to this growing body of evidence, indicating that patients with FD exhibit distinct alterations in duodenal MAM and immune profiles compared to outpatient controls. Furthermore, the immune-microbiome associations present in control populations were absent in FD patients suggesting a loss of host-microbiome homeostasis that may contribute to FD pathophysiology. Our work highlights potential microbial biomarkers which may be a consequence or driver of the mucosal micro-inflammation state which is a characteristic of FD. Future work is required to validate whether these specific microbes are responsible for driving inappropriate host immune responses to inform treatment strategies and assist with disorder diagnosis.

One of the biggest challenges for dairy producers is the substantial variability in final product properties caused by changes in the production environment. In cheese production, this variation is influenced by several factors, particularly the milk base and its pretreatment, which shape the microbiome throughout the process and ultimately affect the cheeses organoleptic characteristics. To examine the impact of three different pre-treatments for pasteurised milk-- microfiltration, protein fortification, and only pasteurisation (control)-- on microbiome dynamics, we generated metagenome sequencing data from 14 cheese production steps across these three production trials at a Danish dairy factory. We constructed three metagenomic co-assemblies, identifying nine high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). Our analysis revealed that a specific strain of Lactococcus lactis dominates the process, while other minor bacterial species persist at very low abundances (<1%), contributing non-negligibly to product properties. Notably, Clostridium tyrobutyricum, a known dairy spoilage bacterium, was present at low levels in pasteurised-only and protein-fortified milk trials but was nearly absent in microfiltered milk. To enhance our analyses, we implemented KHILL, a novel k-mer-based method applied directly to raw sequencing reads, which facilitates metagenomic co-assembly and enables early detection of unwanted microorganisms. Our findings provide industrial dairy producers with a comprehensive view of microbial dynamics during cheese production, offering insights to improve process consistency and product quality.

Amyloids are insoluble protein aggregates with a cross-beta structure, which are traditionally associated with neurodegeneration. Similar structures, named functional amyloids, expressed mostly by microorganisms, play important physiological roles, e.g. bacterial biofilm stabilization. Using a bioinformatics approach, we identify gut microbiome functional amyloids and analyze their potential impact on human health via the gut-brain axis. The results point to taxonomically diverse sources of functional amyloids and their frequent presence in the extracellular space. The retrieved interactions between gut microbiome functional amyloids and human proteins indicate their potential to trigger inflammation, affect transport and signaling processes. We also find a greater relative abundance of bacterial functional amyloids in patients diagnosed with Parkinsons disease and specifically a higher content of the curli amyloid protein, CsgA, in Alzheimers disease patients than in healthy controls. Our results provide a rationale for the tentative link between neurodegeneration and gut bacterial functional amyloids.

sample_q_texts: Acute actinomycosis (AC) is an infectious human disease that affects multiple organs and it is caused by local activation of the mannose-binding lectin (MBL), a lectin that scavenges and removes conserved blood toxins. MBLs virulence was discovered during the 1990s, but the mechanism of action and modes of action in MBL-expressing microorganisms are unknown. The membrane-bound antiviral subunit (Mav1) contains a conserved antiviral tailpiece (V-tail) which forms a hypervariable trans-gyrated alpha helical domain (VGH). Antivirals bind MAV1 and inhibit viral assembly and maturation. In cancer, MAV1 confers increased antiviral activity and MAV1 mutations have been linked to aggressive cancer phenotypes. Here, we constructed a computational computational tool to analyze previous E-Coli and enteropathogenic Squatovirus (S. pyogenes) MAV1 protein structures, along with VGH structures in bacteria and viruses. Furthermore, we used structural knowledge from previous research to predict four more MAV1 VGH domains. We tested these predictions on a MaGV1 bacteriophage, indicating that the MAV1 VGH domain stabilizes the EVI: MAV1 complex. We validated these predictions with experimental results, which revealed that the V-tail structurally remains associated with the MAV1 VGH domain and is therefore stabilised in a structurally unmodified state in MaGV1 phage. This research will pave the way for the use of computational tools to analyze the mechanism of action and the effects of exogenous MBL on bacteria.

Microbial virulence entails multiple virulence mechanisms through the development of extracellular surface proteins. Our work herein shows that the endo-polymorphic virulence factor Hfb proteins target a specific cellular transcription module of the bacterial pericellulary complex in a simple endophytic microbial symbiont, Ampelomyces alliaceus. We show that Hfb1-encoded proteins bind and activate the polyubiquitin-protein H-Glycosyltransferase SAP30. SAP30 is required for both glycolytic and post-translation glycan biosynthesis, and was functionally linked to production of a quorum-quenching GDI. Hfb1-GLCA, Sap30 and Sap31 encode proteases specific for two bacterial glycosides, an N-linked glycolipid-GAG and a glycoprotein and glycoamer. Sequencing analysis confirmed that Sap30-LCC1 in Ampelomyces alliaceus, Hfb1, Hfb2 and GDI are the same glycoside targeting enzymes found in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Further characterization of Sap30 in human and murine M. tuberculosis cell cultures revealed minimal capacity of sap30-LCC1 to interact with the retrovirus, Hsp26. Hfb1 and Hfb2 clearly function as a cutavine. We believe Sap30/LCC1 of Ampelomyces is a fascinating endo-polymorphic virulence factor, that can either increase or reduce virulence according to context. For example, Hfb1, Hfb2 and Sap30-LCC1 were reported to be required for virulence or host cell killing of M. tuberculosis, however Sap30 has no effect on M. tuberculosis virulence. Finally, Sap30 in mutant strains of Ampelomyces (eg. no gdcS, gdcN and snRNA) and murine M. tuberculosis increased Virucidal activity while Sap30 C-peptide in M. tuberculosis reduced Virucidal activity. Our findings serve as a foundation for future studies into microbial virulence.

Stringent Cold Resistance (SCR) is a pathogen-neutral strategy conserved across prokaryotic species. Its presence in various bacterial species around the world has provided an opportunity to design a powerful anti-Salmonella vaccine. However, we lack a specific molecular target for vaccine optimization, and it is uncertain which strains present minimal antigenic burden. To gain insights into the significance of both vaccine strain orogenic and canonical immune response profiles, we analyzed the S. flexneri surface protein (FlexR) from the super-Saccharomyces boulardii strain Chew. The 996A mutation, designated Chew Flexible (cf.) in this study, was determined to be the putative target for booster immunization. Sequence analysis revealed that Chew Flexible strains had reduced FlexR antigenic burden (AF) compared to Chow (CD18-) strains. The presence of a rapid antigen neutralizing ss11 antibody (sr-ap2) and a 2-subunit surface glycoprotein (0a and 2b) response demonstrated robust systemic and high fidelity T cell protection. Further examination of Chew Flexible strains from Southern African megaseptate bacterial isolates (GT83448, GZ-108541, and GZ-110111) identified common features not shared by Chow strains. Those strains predominantly expressed the two canonical S. flexneri SrsT antigen, which in our framework is akin to an Ab subclass I protein.

Influenza viruses infect a diverse array of host cells. C. difficile toxin B (CTBD) is the major toxin produced by many enteric pathogens including C. difficile, STEC, and V. cholerae serotype 3. Previously, it was thought that C. difficile secreted CTBD in the activated secretory stage, while STEC and V. cholerae toxin B does not. However, the proteome of C. difficile secreted proteins was collected from the literature, and only a limited number of enzyme-specific enzymes are known. This study surveyed a comprehensive set of C. difficile secreted proteins in the ProteomeXchange database and also characterized their enzymatic activity. We found that C. difficile secreted proteins were inactive against nearly all select enzymes. Furthermore, non-required enzymes appear to be genetically equivalent to the known ones, whereas non-sensor enzymatic activities are unique for at least one identified enzyme. Our findings show that only a small subset of C. difficile secreted proteins are physiologically active against the key targets of C. difficile toxin.

STEC toxin A is a known virulence factor in Oysters in shellfish aquaculture which is mainly responsible for adhesion and phagocytosis of oysters. It is attached to the cytoplasmic domain of the coat protein using a complex adhesive coat structure and secreted as a trimer in the sea water for host cells.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa, an obligate anaerobe, is now recognised as a global zoonosis, and its pathogenic risk is increasing due to cross-species transmission to humans. However, the role of classical bacterial pathogen-derived proteins in pathogenicity is unclear, and the mechanisms through which such proteins function remain poorly defined. Here we report that a highly homologous form of the P. aeruginosa penicillin binding protein (Pbp) regulates virulence. We generated RsuR125, which encodes a novel Pbp analogue derived from the P. aeruginosa PgrG-like protein. Using recombinant protein expression in mammalian cells and Western blotting, we demonstrate that RsuR125 inhibits vibrio haemolysin (Vhb) production and confers P. aeruginosa resistance to antimicrobial agents. Molecular docking experiments and quantitative molecular dynamics simulations reveal that RsuR125 binds to vibriomanas host binding motif (HBM) portion of the P. aeruginosa membrane fusion complex (Fmc). VirB-Vhb dimerisation triggers the highly glycosylated HBM-binding reaction, and this reaction is inhibited by riboswitches. RsuR125 binds and interacts with key sites in vibriophagic process and modulates the response of the cells of P. aeruginosa to interfering agents. Additionally, RsuR125-induced downregulation of virulence genes may account for the hypervirulence observed in xenogeneic isolates. Taken together, this study reveals the essential role of extracellular bacterial antigen in the development of severe vibriopneumonia, and of the virulence of this pathogen in human disease, through its modulation of the bacterium-host cell surface interaction. Lastly, our results reveal that P. aeruginosa RsuR125 and P. aeruginosa VibIcB -DNA binding protein (VibIs) are active efflux pump subunits that provide P. aeruginosa cell wall permeability with an export ability.

TitleProteins binding flaviviruses and papillons: structural insight into entry, unligand binding, functions and pathophysiology.

ReferenceWang J, Chen Y, Lu Z, Zhong X, Liu S, Xiao C, Pan X, et al. Defects in outer membrane surface glycoprotein (PgrG) induce VirB-Vhb dimer formation and cell wall permeability to enhance virulence in pseudomonas aeruginosa. PLoS One. 2016;11(6):e0158347. PMID27684342 DOI 10.1371/JOURNAL.MOAR

To mitigate the risk of bacterial infections in humans, vaccines and/or therapeutic therapies containing antibiotic compounds would need to be designed that are highly efficient against multi-drug resistant bacteria (MRSA) without giving rise to secondary bacterial resistance on secondary drug targets. Here we show that the engineered bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa TNP-4, which is an engineered fitness-maintenance secretion system modified to produce a cationic toxin (nanobodia 2), can be engineered to form stable, self-assembly structures such as small rigid nanoaggregates by the equally ubiquitous bacterial nutrient factor Nan T and its derivative Nan T-1. Nan T-1 is found in the vicinity of Ec 13B, an essential member of a plasmid-encoded iron regulatory network, while Nan T binds both of these polypeptides through a novel co-translational interaction of the pre-protein complex. Nan T-1 is also found in large numbers in the upper side of the outer membrane of TNP-4 and other biofilms, which suggests that Nan T-1 might also regulate biofilm formation. Through imaging and TEM analyses, we show that Nan T-1 specifically binds, and in fact acts as a physical stabilizer for the two polypeptides of Ec 13B-based quorum sensing systems. This discovery resolves a long debated thermodynamic scenario of Ec 13B-based quorum sensing, in which it is known that Ec 13B-based systems are highly tolerant to the presence of quorum sensing inhibitors without undergoing any shift in the expression profile. The bacterial system depicted here shows specific sensitivity to environmental factors including the pH gradient and small organic molecules. In this instance, the new structure also allows for distinct regulation of Ec 13B-based quorum sensing with longer intracellular signaling period due to the phase transition effect of Ec 13B-based sensing in the lower side of the outer membrane and we anticipate this has previously unpredicted implications for the bacterial biology. The nanobodia-active quorum sensing system of TNP-4 and Ec 13B has been named Eco13TnP4-Ec13B-Nan T-1, and Nano T and Nan T-1 have been awarded "Notable Papers". Immune response to a dengue infection in mice expressing C3b C" terminal complement component in the skin, designated staphylococcal-like (SL), is unique and remains unexplored. Staphylococcal adhesion to the human Fc receptor FcRI is supported by the molecular signature of its lysozyme domain. Staphylococcal defense against staphylococcal pathogens, even those without the bacteria-targeting portion of the tail, suggests that the Fc receptor plays a role in Staphylococcal adherence. The SL staphylococci have been reported to disrupt immune tolerance, leading to bacterial virulence in mice. However, studies indicate that the Srf-deficient background strain provides more immune-competent mice than the SL strain, necessitating the need for better understanding of staphylococcal immune responses in cells after FcR binding. Here we show that the staphylococci are blocked by FcRI by non-glycosylated repetitive M domain (MR) of FcRI but not by FcRI Ig domain (FI). MR-FcRI, like the smaller fragments of STAF01 and STAF02, binds many FcRI molecules with low affinities (K = 1.4 x 10-9 M). Our data indicate that the receptor-FcRI engagement is ineffective. Consistent with this idea, we report that internalization into FcRI of STAF020, a mouse orthologous toxin, results in the inability of Staf to cause a systemic infection in mice due to failure of the FcyR domain to fully engage the receptor. The target cell internalization of STAF020 is prevented by mAb but not activated by FcRI. Importantly, it is previously reported that STAF020 and Staf share conserved amino-acid residues in the firefly light-harvesting complexes of various mobile units (STAF01, STAF02, STAF03 and STAF04), including amino-acid substitutions consistent with STAF mutations. Thus, STAF020 represents the full-length toxin with a different firefly light-harvesting unit, that is, a tetramer of STAF02 inserted within the STAF020 repeating domain. These findings highlight the importance of homologous virulence and co-expression analyses to understand innate immunity and bacterial evasion mechanisms.

SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENTThrombocytopenia during covid-19 infection is often associated with a decreased Fc receptor (FcR) affinity. Current work has found that FcRI-Srf bind to STAF02C0023

BackgroundThe majority of staphylococcal pneumonias in adolescents treated in Ethiopia under Staphylococcal Pneumonia treatment program was polymicrobial, with Staphylococcal pyogenis most often the pathogen. Myeloperoxidase (MPO) oxidative burst, a signature pro-inflammatory property found on staphylococci, has been described in molecular descriptors for pneumococcal bacterial pathogenicity. To better understand the factors behind the inability of the respiratory pathogen Serratia marcescens to induce MPO oxidant activity, we performed a comparative microbial proteomics approach for S. marcescens and S. aureus strains. Proteomic methods should contribute directly to metabolic pathways which have been established by correlation with literature sources and the validation of experimental concepts or theories. Following sample pretreatment, samples were separated and subjected to ProteoFinder VIP Pro-Tn-proteome profiling to identify potential MPO production or more likely Proteome-specific protein domain analysis, using a curated reference. Protein domains were then selected and functionally characterised based on UniProt CB [1].

ResultsFrom these initial steps, a first group of 70 potential MPO-related domains was identified in the S. marcescens reference of ProteoFinderVIP, with putative binding motifs for oxidoreductase and prolyl hydroxylase. From these, 28 proteins with two or more domains were selected to characterise the potential MPO-effector effector domain content of S. marcescens by profiling them against CB, where ~20 domains had a minimum protein-inhibitor concentration.

ConclusionsThese results establish an increased potential MPO reactive domain pattern in the threedomain-large-pore and oxidoreductase-2 domains. Additionally, the 10 domains with the potential to be targets for investigational anti-S. marcescens therapies were also identified, supporting the involvement of MPO effector enzyme activities in adaptive immunity against MRSA in the respiratory tract.

Streptococcus pneumoniae (S. pneumoniae) is a common bacterium that colonizes the respiratory tract throughout life and has the ability to evict acquired antigenic variation from the mucosal environment through the generation of inhibitory factors. It is a model for our immune system because S. pneumoniae manipulates its TCR-T cell environment in various tissues of the body to create highly diverse immunity, one of the hallmarks of developing immune phenotypes and therefore generating and deploying adaptive immune responses. In this study we use data from the 2015 Strep Screening Study (SST) to define the RNA viruses, the clinical phenotype and serotype (or major histocompatibility complex [MHC] version) of human pneumococcal infection in Northern California to characterize their potential associations with S. pneumoniae pathogenesis. RNA viruses isolated from 284 samples of stable isolates of Pneumococcal pneumonia (Pn) were sequenced for viruses from five human pneumococcal serotypes, M1, M3, M4, M42, and M5, and six types of Escherichia coli having a similar genome to S. pneumoniae. We found 176, or 64% of the 284 samples, were infected by S. pneumoniae serotype M3 and 38, or 14%, were infected by M3 serotype only. None of the serotypes were infected by M4, and these serotypes were collectively infected by other pneumococcal serotypes. Genotyping by type was not associated with viral or clinical severity, but many S. pneumoniae serotypes carried risk haplotypes that differed between non-seronegative and seropositive infections. However, the most consistent association was identified between RNA viruses and allergic type reactions, so we suggest an adverse immune response is required for the virus to generate the subpopulation of lytic membrane proteins, an anti-M3 or the T cell-interacting proteins, and to produce the highly protein-rich, serotype-specific, spike protein component responsible for hemolytic community production, which stabilizes the immune response through its antigenic capability. Our data suggest a novel clinical phenotype with mild symptoms that emerge when the body recognizes the S. pneumoniae spike protein and could affect a major portion of the human population. This study demonstrates the importance of closely understanding viral heterogeneity to develop targeted vaccines or therapeutic inhibitors or agents to counter this epidemic as global levels of infection increase.

Enterotoxin B (Etb) is one of the most commonly occurring proteins in Staphylococcus aureus. Etb is a neurotoxin produced by Staphylococcus aureus, with the A subunit containing the binding site for enterotoxins. Staphylococcus aureus is typically found naturally in the human skin and in the genital region and rarely colonizes the gastrointestinal tract. While, over the years, Etb is reported in all types of staphylococcal infections as a major pathogen. In spite of the extensive studies of various research and development works on this protein, there are still many important aspects that we need to address. Hence, this review tries to understand the modes of interactions between the host immune responses and this protein. While, many researchers have tried to represent these interactions using various models, this article takes into account the effect of etb on the bacterial proteins and its receptors. The proteins and receptors of interest include cell surface proteins, membrane and intra-cellular proteins and receptors, and host immune response at the site of infection and after infection. The results indicate that etb can act as a factor to induce pro-inflammatory response or inhibit the early stages of inflammatory reactions of the human body.

Main Message

The survival of Staphylococcus aureus remains a serious global health concern as it is the leading cause of infections across the world. The current efforts to engineer harmless Staphylococcus aureus has resulted in emergence of antibiotic resistant strains of the species. Staphylococci have been explored as bioengineered therapeutics for their potential as therapeutic antibiotics as they can have clinically useful biotechnological functions such as antimicrobial activity and protein expression. However, little has been known about the modes of interactions between Staphylococci and their main protein sources. This review analyzes a large number of potential interactions between Staphylococci and their factors to provide a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms by which Staphylococci interact with their factors and target their factors in a search for novel bacteria for therapeutic applications.
