Glycocins are a growing family of ribosomally synthesized and posttranslationally modified peptides that are O- and/or S-glycosylated. Using a sequence similarity network of putative glycosyltransferases, the tht biosynthetic gene cluster was identified in the genome of Thermoanaerobacterium thermosaccharolyticum. ThtA is the precursor peptide to a member of the glycocin F family of glycocins. Like other members of this family, the glycosyltransferase (ThtS) encoded in the biosynthetic gene cluster adds N-acetyl-glucosamine to both Ser and Cys residues of ThtA. S-linked glycosylation has been shown to be chemically and enzymatically resistant to cleavage and therefore ThtS may be a valuable starting point for engineering efforts. The glycocin derived from ThtA, which we name thermoglycocin, was structurally characterized. Thermoglycocin is unique in that in addition to two nested disulfide bonds, it contains an additional disulfide bond creating a C-terminal loop. Unexpectedly, ThtA lacks the common double glycine motif that denotes a C39-peptidase leader peptide cleavage site. Based on AlphaFold3 modeling, we postulate that cleavage between the leader and core peptide occurs instead at a GK motif. This study adds to the small number of characterized glycocins, employs AlphaFold3 to aid in predicting the structure of the mature peptide product, and suggests a common naming convention similar to that established for lanthipeptides.

One sentence summaryThermoglycocin is a novel glycocin derived from the thermophile Thermoanaerobacterium thermosaccharolyticum, containing three disulfide bonds, O- and S-GlcNAcylation, and is postulated to have a unique C39 protease cut site.

Staphylococcus aureus is among the leading causes of hospital-acquired infections. Critical to S. aureus biology and pathogenesis are the cell wall-anchored glycopolymers wall teichoic acids (WTA). Approximately one-third of S. aureus isolates decorates WTA with a mixture of 1,4- and {beta}1,4-N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc), which requires the dedicated glycosyltransferases TarM and TarS, respectively. Environmental conditions, such as high salt concentrations, affect the abundance and ratio of 1,4- and {beta}1,4-GlcNAc WTA decorations, thereby impacting biological properties such as antibody binding and phage infection. To identify regulatory mechanisms underlying WTA glycoswitching, we screened 1,920 S. aureus mutants (Nebraska Transposon Mutant Library) by immunoblotting for differential expression of WTA-linked 1,4- or {beta}1,4-GlcNAc using specific monoclonal antibody Fab fragments. Three two-component systems (TCS), GraRS, ArlRS, and AgrCA, were among the 230 potential hits. Using isogenic TCS mutants, we demonstrated that ArlRS is essential for WTA {beta}1,4-GlcNAc decoration through regulation of tarM but not tarS. ArlRS regulated tarM expression through the transcriptional regulator MgrA, which was responsive to Mg2+, but not Na+. Importantly, ArlRS-mediated regulation of WTA glycosylation affected S. aureus interaction with the innate receptor langerin and lysis by {beta}1,4-GlcNAc-dependent phages. Since WTA represents a promising target for future immune-based treatments and vaccines, our findings provide important insight to align targeting strategies with the S. aureus WTA glycosylation patterns during infection.

ImportanceStaphylococcus aureus is a common colonizer of mucosal surfaces, but is also a frequent cause of severe infections in humans. Development of antibiotic resistance complicates treatment of S. aureus infections, increasing the need for antibiotic alternatives such as vaccines and therapies with bacterial viruses also known as phages. Wall teichoic acids (WTA) are abundantly-expressed glycosylated structures of the S. aureus cell wall that have gained attention as a promising target for new treatments. Importantly, WTA glycosylation patterns show variation depending on environmental conditions, thereby impacting phage binding and interaction with host factors, such as antibodies and innate pattern-recognition receptors. Here, we show that the two-component system ArlRS through its effector MgrA is involved in regulation of WTA glycosylation by responding to environmental changes in Mg2+ concentration. These findings may support the design of new treatment strategies that target WTA glycosylation patterns of S. aureus during infection.

Shiga toxin types 1 (Stx1) and 2 (Stx2), produced by Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) and Shigella dysenteriae, are key virulence factors responsible for severe foodborne diseases, such as hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). The receptors for Stxs are Gb3 and P1 glycotope, which contain the Gal1[->]4Gal epitope and are synthesized by human 1,4-galactosyltransferase (A4galt). Stx-related infections pose a global public health challenge, owing to the limited therapeutic options due to the restricted use of antibiotics. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop novel therapeutic strategies. This study proposes an innovative strategy utilizing exosomes derived from CHO-Lec2 cells, which were modified with Functional-Spacer-Lipid (FSL) conjugates bearing the Gb3 carbohydrate epitope (exo-Gb3-FSL). Flow cytometry analysis confirmed the presence of Gal1[->]4Gal disaccharides on exo-Gb3-FSL constructs, enabling them to bind Stx1. Moreover, using CHO-Lec2 cells evaluated the ability of exo-Gb3-FSL agents to bind Stx1 and protect these cells from Stx1-mediated cytotoxicity. For Stx1-treated CHO-Lec2 cells, increased cell survival was observed when using 25 {micro}M exo-Gb3-FSL constructs, compared to control cells. These findings highlight the potential of exosome-based anti-Stx1 agents as promising alternatives to conventional therapies. This innovative strategy may provide novel directions for studies on Stx1 neutralization, offering a valuable strategy for the treatment of Stx-related diseases.

Highlights- Exo-Gb3-FSL constructs hold Stx1 binding Gal1[->]4Gal epitope.
- Stx1 was effectively bound by exo-Gb3-FSL constructs.
- Exo-Gb3-FSL protected CHO-Lec2 cells from Stx1.
- Exo-Gb3-FSL is a promising anti-Stx1 agent.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a bacterial wall-less human pathogen and the etiological agent of atypical pneumonia and tracheobronchitis in both adults and children. M. pneumoniae infectivity, gliding motility and adherence to host target respiratory epithelial cells are mediated by adhesin proteins P1 and P40/P90 forming a transmembrane complex that binds to sialylated oligosaccharides human cell ligands. Here we report the cryo-EM structure of P1 bound to the Fab fragment of monoclonal antibody P1/MCA4, which stops gliding and induces detachment of motile M. pneumoniae cells. On the contrary, polyclonal antibodies generated against the N-domain of P1 or against the whole ectodomain of P40/P90 have little or no effects on adhesion or motility. The epitope of P1/MCA4, centred on loop Thr1426-Asp1438 in the small C-terminal domain of P1, is inaccessible to antibodies in the "open" conformation of the adhesion complex, when ready for attachment to sialylated oligosaccharides. Mutations in the highly conserved Engelman motifs found in the transmembrane helix of P40/P90 also alter adhesion and motility. During the attachment/detachment cycle of the adhesion complex, the C-terminal domain of P1 experiences large conformational rearrangements that are hindered by the antibodies against the domain. Interfering with the gliding of mycoplasma cells suggests new ways to confront M. pneumoniae infections.

Bovine mastitis, a prevalent and costly disease affecting dairy cows, severely impacts milk production, quality, and cow health and poses significant challenges to the dairy industry worldwide. Traditional treatment strategies relying on antibiotics face concerns of antibiotic resistance and residual antibiotic residues in dairy products. Therefore, there is an urgent need for innovative and sustainable approaches. Our study undertakes a preliminary investigation into the formulation and efficacy of a GMO-based antibiotic-free treatment in fighting Bovine mastitis. We propose to use the bioengineered defensin Nisin PV as the antimicrobial to specifically target the causative pathogen Staphylococcus aureus. To disrupt the biofilm formation, we have leveraged the potency of DNaseI. By hacking the quorum sensing technique of Staphylococcus aureus, our proposed genetically modified bacteria would sense the presence of pathogens and initiate their eradication by producing Nisin PV and DNaseI. Results show the efficacy of DNase I against bacterial biofilm formation, in addition to the efficacy of our proposed sensor, which is based on the agr quorum sensing system of Staphylococcus aureus, a major cause of bovine mastitis. Molecular dynamics and simulations show that our choice of the bacterial defensin, Nisin PV, is less susceptible to cleavage by bacterial strains resistant to the native bacteriocin Nisin A. Additionally, we theoretically propose a lysis-based kill switch to ensure the release of the therapeutic components. The solution proposed in this study has the potential to offer a sustainable and effective alternative to antibiotic-based treatments. Implementation of bioengineered defensins could reduce disease incidence, minimize economic losses, and promote responsible antimicrobial stewardship in the dairy industry.

Klebsiella pneumoniae is listed as a critical priority pathogen by the WHO due to prevalent extended-spectrum {beta}-lactamase and carbapenem resistance and high mortality rates Hypervirulent K. pneumoniae (hvKp) causes life-threatening infections in immunocompetent individuals, while classical K. pneumoniae (cKp) causes nosocomial infections in immunosuppressed patients. The convergence of hypervirulence with antibiotic resistance is now a major global health threat. Using a murine pulmonary infection model, we show that hvKp resisted clearance despite significant neutrophil recruitment. Using clinical hvKp and cKp isolates, bone marrow derived neutrophils, cell biology, pharmacology and imaging (both light and electron microscopy) in ex vivo assays revealed that the hvKp hypermucoviscous capsule prevents bacterial recognition and neutrophil activation, blocking ROS production, degranulation, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) formation. In the absence of capsule ({Delta}wcaJ) or hypermucoid capsule determinants ({Delta}rmpADC), hvKp activates neutrophils, leading to degranulation, NET formation and bacterial killing. While superimposing the absence of O-antigen ({Delta}rfb) on the {Delta}wcaJ abrogates degranulation, neutrophils still elaborate NETs that eliminate the {Delta}wcaJ/{Delta}rfb mutant at high efficiency. This suggests that O-antigen is a double-edged sword, functioning as a PAMP triggering neutrophil degranulation yet assisting the pathogen to evade NET-mediated destruction. These findings shed light on the mechanism underpinning immune evasion by the hypervirulent capsule in hvKp.

Infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus are closely linked to its ability to secure essential nutrients, including iron, which is extracted from the heme of human hemoglobin (Hb) through the iron-regulated surface determinant (Isd) system. The compound 4-[[2-[[5- (1H-indol-3-yl)-1,3,4-oxadiazol-2-yl]sulfanyl]acetyl]amino]benzoate (C35) was recently identified as a new potential antimicrobial agent for its ability to bind Hb and hamper its interaction with the staphylococcal hemophore IsdB in vitro. Here, we show that C35 inhibits S. aureus growth by specifically targeting the hemophore-driven iron acquisition system. Our findings confirm both the potential of C35 as a first-in-class protein-protein interaction inhibitor with antimicrobial activity, and the effectiveness of targeting hemophores as a strategy to inhibit S. aureus growth. To gain information for drug discovery purposes, the X-ray structure of Hb in the presence of the compound was solved. Unexpectedly, we discovered that, rather than the predicted binding pose, the molecule binds to tetrameric Hb in a cleft between the alpha subunits, stabilizing an R2 relaxed Hb conformation. This triggered further investigation of the effect of C35 on Hb functional properties, which showed a pronounced left-shift activity on oxygen binding curve (i.e., it strongly increases the Hb oxygen affinity). These results highlight C35 as a promising dual-acting compound with both antimicrobial activity and the ability to modulate Hb function through non-covalent stabilization of a high-affinity state.

Author SummaryStaphylococcus aureus is a dangerous bacterium that can cause severe infections in humans. To grow and survive it needs iron, which it steals from our red blood cells by taking it from hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in the blood. In this study, we focused on a small molecule, called C35, that blocks the interaction between hemoglobin and a key bacterial protein involved in heme acquisition. We found that C35 strongly inhibits the growth of S. aureus when hemoglobin is the only available source of iron, showing a potential new method to starve the pathogen and consequently fight the infection. Surprisingly, we also found that C35 increases the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen. This dual action makes C35 a unique molecule for future therapeutic development, with potential applications both as a new antimicrobial agent and in the treatment of diseases related to hemoglobin function.

Executive control, the mental processes that sustain executive dysfunction, include self-initiated action, prioritization, problem-solving, and context awareness. Given our current understanding of executive function, the extent to which cortical regions are required to support the executive function is an important question to study in order to increase our understanding of executive dysfunction. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to quantify the cortical areas with functioning at the fronto-parietal junction (FPJ) and subcallosal cortex (SCC) as a function of amygdala activation in attentional monitoring. First, we validated the use of resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to map cortical activity in the FPJ and SCC. We then compared resting-state activity measured from each of the three-dimensional fMRI to attentional task performance (e.g., reaction time, accuracy, detection). In addition, we confirmed that resting-state fMRI spatial resolution matches the FST voxel resolution. As the visual working memory (VWM) increases in working duration, its accessibility is the key for maintaining the observed increases in cognition (Broca 2008; gerscher 2019). However, its capacity is inconsistent, and difficulties in adopting tasks with different demands can trigger the inability to maintain access to such storage capacity. As VWM is modulated by the mismatch between the capacity and task demands, including the role of different attentional biases (Arazi-Reginato 2017). The development of tools, such as Cognitive Load Checker (CLC), has allowed obtaining novel studies about the malleability of attentional biases in working memory. The aim of this study is to combine the CLC based VWM-enhancing strategy with a new attentional dataset of 237 participants in 4 tasks: cued matching, continuous presentation of non-target items on demand, retroactive competition, and go/no go task. CLC and our novel attentional approach will be applied, using 50 stimuli in 5 conditions. Variables of interest were: recognition times, errors, and productivity (percentage of correct responses). Cognitive loads across conditions were associated to different recall strategies, with highest scores in demanding tasks. Generalization and vigilance were analyzed separately using cluster analysis. Task variable were associated to specific cognitive biases, with generalizations in distractibility; vigilance in proactive interference; and sequencing in proactive bias. Our method was more efficient than CLC in distinguishing between cognitive biases, thus providing additional information about their application in work-like or cognitively demand tasks. Our findings indicate that the cognitive biases interact with tasks load as well as the different attentional biases. It is also shown that generalizations and vigilance are rather separately associated with behavioral variations, with global attentional biases contributing most of the difficulty in the mastery of working memory.

Humans who are sensitive to shift work can suffer severe sleep disruptions, leading to fatigue and impaired performance in multi-tasking activities, such as computer programming. While changes in sleep architecture and working memory are thought to be involved, there is no molecular understanding of how sleep and cognitive work across tasks simultaneously. In the absence of poor sleep outcomes for more generalized cognitive dysfunction, we use multiplex imaging to follow brain changes after an intensive night of severe sleep deprivation. By performing longitudinal EEG-MRI on 58 participants from different birth cohorts for six months, we find that, across all ages, critical sleep episodes, characterized by sparse sleep, are accompanied by persistent sleep architecture changes involving slow wave sleep, preceding wake and opposite wake sleep, and frontal lateralized sleep, followed by wakefulness. The variants for cognitive processes differed, as the severity of sleep deprivation influenced the ability of participants to correctly identify more difficult tasks across tasks after sleep deprivation. Furthermore, bloodwork from these participants showed neurochemical shifts due to sleep deprivation, with the exception of changes in testosterone. Our findings suggest that sleep architecture and cognitive processes must be closely intertwined to understand the mechanisms of cognitive dysfunction resulting from sleep loss.

Past research suggests that changes in episodic and working memory (WM) regions and posterior cingulate (PCC) can influence one another, often occurring in concert. Yet, understanding the role of PCC in predicting those changes has been hampered by a lack of well-characterized task-specific covariates, such as demands. In our study, to address this, we conducted a series of fMRI studies and a meta-analysis to determine the role of PCC, specifically a recent FC1c voxel in the frontal-temporal cortex, in association with changes in WM and working memory, regarding four cognitive functions: visual object sorting, visual object perseveration, visual reading speed, and repetition priming. Results showed that the PCC was more active for visual sorting and sorting-based WM, indicating a higher functional connectivity between these functions, whereas it was more active for reading speed, suggesting the PCC plays a distinct role in these functions. Our findings suggest that changes in PFC-based WM can indeed influence the PCC, potentially highlighting the non-linear role of PFC in cognition.

The cognitive impact of long-term social isolation has long been recognised, but its effect on brain function is still not completely understood. In this article we review recent findings from studies in rhesus monkeys and rhesus macaques. They confirm that the metabolic responses to social deprivation are less severe in monkeys than in rhesus macaques. Brain regions that are recruited during motor and emotional behaviours display less robust alterations during long-term social isolation, yet these regions are also specifically disrupted by social stress to other monkey species and remain stable over time. These findings suggest that long-term social isolation may have many other biological consequences. Social isolation has a small impact on spatial working memory, but this does not translate to increased memory capacity. Long-term social isolation disrupts emotional reactivity and behavioural flexibility, a finding that has some precedent in the emotional and behavioural consequences of post-traumatic stress disorder. To suggest that social isolation has biological impact requires further experimentation to identify molecular targets and specific targets within the brain.

We examined whether neural activity and cognitive state modulate attention using EEG. In four 17-day series of behavioral experiments performed in a single session, during intensive three-hour sessions of training in the Task VR program, college students evaluated visually presented objects in the VR environment and performed the Stroop test at baseline and then during the training. Attention, perceived attentional effort, and EEG activity of the fMRI consistent with structural changes in the prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). A series of three-item tasks examining visual tasks efficiency when cognitive state changes during the Stroop task, were performed on weekdays, and examined the neurobehavioral effects of the dual task environment on the efficiency of the first (CST) and second (SST) tasks, through automatic EEG and ERP bi-directional correlation analysis. The results showed that task stress has a cumulative effect on the ability to attend to only one item. This negative effect of the alternating workload of consecutive tasks on the response time (RT) was reduced when the first task and the second (SST) task were performed on consecutive days at different times (k). On days with two or three consecutive sessions, training proved to be more efficient, while on days with a regular single training session, it was not. EEG data confirmed that the constructive effect of the alternating workload is not effective and decreases due to the likelihood of positive learning.

Key challenges for aging include cognitive decline, alterations in memory and cognition, and neurodegenerative disorders like Alzheimers and depression. While a majority of studies have evaluated the role of brain aging on memory functions, they fail to investigate the relationship between neurocognitive impairments and aging, let alone the unique impact of aging on those impairments. Our previous studies have revealed that specific and unique genetic modifiers of brain aging may be determined by individual differences in cognitive function, potentially affecting individual risk of brain aging and disease vulnerability, and sensory sensitivity and precision. Our current work is dedicated to (1) exploring the impact of age-related brain aging on cognitive performance of elderly individuals with low cognitive abilities, and (2) investigating the unique relationships between brain aging and cognitive impairment. Using task-irrelevant delayed reproduction (TRD) tasks that measure error propagation, we identified a substantial effect of aging on error propagation speed, correlating with age and poor index scores. We also observed a trend in brain aging predictors related to EEG biomarkers (i.e., beta, theta, and band power), exploring the spatial distribution of individual brain variables and their interaction. The results suggest that the aging process may not affect all potential predictors for ERD, yet an interaction between aging and age-related cognitive impairment may lead to substantial cognitive degradation, potentially elevating neuropsychiatric conditions. Our findings underscore the need to develop more advanced and sensitive tools for training new and aging populations, emphasizing the importance of refining existing memory and information integration tasks. Moreover, we emphasize the need for comprehensive longitudinal research that includes both sensory and non-sensory traits, recognizing that every human brain has distinct memory and perceptual processing capabilities.

Key Points

In this study, four cohorts of young adults completed a brief attention span task and a behavioral measure assessing anxiety toward certain aspects of unfamiliar activities. Individual cognitive and affective profiles emerged from data collected from the headphones used in the task. The participants who had a focus/self-control impairment were particularly focused on the environment in their environment, while the participants who had a focus/self-control impairment anxiety, scored higher on a brief anxiety rating tool and lower on personal contentment. The anxiety related affective profile was not stable for individuals but was described in terms of a phobia style, a group who worked together and diverged from the task and displayed an interest in one another.

HighlightsStudies of social functioning in the age-old question of whether it really matters which it is, and how. Study reveals how meaningful life events, relationships and states of mind change over a lifetime. Study reveals the significance of focusing on one task for that moment and whether that remains relevant to a future individual. Study explores the meaning that aspects of daily living and nature have on quality of life and whether this was related to spending time with other people.

ObjectiveTo establish and reproduce plasticity thresholds associated with age-related changes in attention.MethodsWe evaluated learning in a fMRI task measuring the influence of a protective measure task on executive attention while varying stimulation conditions over time. We examined effects of age (18-year olds, 30-year olds and 50-year olds) and stimulus modality (visual or auditory) while differing the degree of weighting on training stimuli within a conditioned "block" task. ResultsIn both perceptual training and visual word recognition tasks, older and younger adults (as well as binational adults) were more efficient in learning a block-specific, but not a category-specific word prime. In the block-specific perceptual task, only young and older adults (but not binational adults) benefited from higher stimulus weights during the block training phase. In the block recognition task, only young adults (but not older adults) benefited from higher stimulus weights during the block recognition task, but this effect disappeared with aging. The FSTA showed significant age differences, but in auditory stimuli only and across generations. Next-level processing (NLP) models indicated that older adults' capacity for perceptual prediction in a categorical based task shifted with age, while young adults performance shifted with generation and other behavioral measures. Lastly, as a counterpoint to previous findings in other contexts, studies demonstrated that for both age groups, fMRI-trained older adults (compared to older adults or young adults) were better at visual detection but worse at auditory detection, suggesting a trade-off between perceptual gains in older adults and age-related decreases in auditory performance.

ImportanceDespite considerable evidence of age-related plasticity in brain circuits, fMRI has yet to document such age-related shifts in performance. We introduce the Potential-Shift-Following Test, which tracks neural responses in a counterfactual framework, as a new technique for quantifying changes in neural activity between different conditions in a neurological change experiment. Applying this paradigm to a factor-manipulated fMRI task showed a surprising result: older adults experienced a shift in their performance at cross-modal repetition, without a similar change in performance at cross-modal learning.

Reduced cognitive resources to facilitate complex problem-solving often result in weak abstract processing and inefficient risk-taking behavior. Here, we investigated the influence of stress on attentional processes during long-term-exposure to stressful events, followed by a reversal of that stressor, in 23 young healthy participants and 20 older adult participants. In a timed go/no-go reaction time task, stressor durations (duration1 and duration2) were randomized by e-tape or analog, respectively. Regression analyses revealed an effect of duration1 on stressor duration on picture judgment accuracy and speed, and an effect of stressor duration on response time of picture judgment. T-tests showed a significant difference in age groups, however, this effect depended on stressor duration. Results were supported by changes in event-related potentials (ERPs) in the automated version of the go/no-go reaction time task. Irrespective of stressor duration, a stressor that was first presented at short intervals (duration1=5 min) led to a delayed mismatch at n400 (NMSSD). Nonetheless, older participants showed less deficit than younger participants, even after a reversal of stressor. These findings suggest that stress-induced attenuation of efﬁcacious neurocognitive strategies might be an important mechanism accounting for adult cognitive decline.
sample_p_texts: Working memory (WM) decline in ageing may be related to increases in "neural noise", potentially reflected in the EEG aperiodic exponent. We reanalysed previously published data to investigate age-related differences in the aperiodic exponent during verbal WM and its relationship with neural inefficiency. EEG was recorded from 24 younger (18-35 years) and 30 older adults (50-86 years) during a modified Sternberg task with 1-letter, 3-letter, and 5-letter load conditions. Younger adults consistently demonstrated steeper aperiodic slopes than older adults, though this difference was less pronounced in frontal regions during retention. Unexpectedly, both age groups showed decreased (i.e. flattened) aperiodic exponents during retention relative to fixation, with minimal load-dependent effects. Notably, the relationship between task-related exponent changes and WM performance was complex and dependent on the exponent at fixation, particularly in older adults. Finally, flatter exponents during fixation and late retention were associated with greater neural inefficiency during stimulus processing, reflected by increased P3b amplitudes without corresponding WM performance improvements. These findings suggest that flatter exponents are associated with less efficient neural processing and that older adults flexibly modulate their aperiodic exponent during retention to support WM performance.

Although macaques and marmosets are both primates of choice for studying the brain mechanisms of cognition, they differ in key aspects of anatomy and behavior. Interestingly, recent connectomic analysis revealed that strong top-down projections from the prefrontal cortex to the posterior parietal cortex, present in macaques and important for executive function, are absent in marmosets. Here, we propose a consensus mapping that bridges the two species cortical atlases and allows for direct area-to-area comparison of their connectomes, which are then used to build comparative computational large-scale modeling of the frontoparietal circuit for working memory. We found that the macaque model exhibits resilience against distractors, a prerequisite for normal working memory function. By contrast, the marmoset model is sensitive to distractibility commonly observed behaviorally in this species. Surprisingly, this contrasting trend can be swapped by scaling intrafrontal and frontoparietal connections. Finally, the relevance to primate ethology and evolution is discussed.

We developed a new experimental approach to compare how attentional orienting facilitates retrieval from working memory (WM) and long-term memory (LTM), and how selective attention within these two memory types impacts incoming sensory information processing. In three experiments with healthy young adults, retrospective attention cues prioritized an item represented in WM or LTM. Participants then retrieved a memory item or performed a perceptual task. The retrocue was informative for the retrieval task but not for the perceptual task. Attentional orienting benefited performance for both WM and LTM, with stronger effects for WM. Eye-tracking revealed significant gaze shifts and microsaccades correlated with attention in WM but not LTM. Visual discrimination of unrelated visual stimuli was consistently improved for items matching attended WM locations. Similar effects occurred at LTM locations but less consistently. The findings suggest potent and at least partly dissociable attention-orienting processes for different memory types.

Leukemia cells utilize streptavidin-1-streptavidin-10 (StrepSA-1-SA-10) linked to immobilized forms of soluble thrombospondin-2 (Sest2) and surface displayed human leukocyte antigen-DR3 (HLA-DR3) to form Stremadriii: layer-like intercellular structures capable of producing leukemia (Leukemia) invasion invasion factor (LIF). The Leustridioon is an opportunistic apicomplexan pathogen mainly found in tropical regions, capable of establishing invasive secondary infections. The amphibiophilia of Strepadriii poses a threat to mankind, with its potential pathogenic capability estimated at tens of millions of people per year. The bacterium is transmitted via the salivary gland into the human alimentary tract through a new bypass route, threatening the human gastrointestinal tract. Despite their hydatid parasitisism, many strains are now controlled by antibiotic resistance.

Here, we provide an active site-directed computational model of Strepadriii - STTP, containing KDNAs S2-B and S2-C while not hindering the microbe's pathogenic potential, enabling an effective regulation of their production to selectively target the microbe without inducing resistance.

The prevalence of Mycobacterium fortuitum endosymbionts in mammals remains largely understudied, largely driven by challenges in culturing these bacteria, even from natural hosts. In this work, we show that the M. fortuitum genera endosymbiont, M. furry disorder (MFD) and M. mercurialis, accumulate in wild mammals and harbor the primary rRNA gene with bacterial sequence similarity and molecular phylogeny close to the MB120 lineage of M. fortuitum, indicating high sequence similarity. Additionally, MFD and M. mercurialis also co-carried a tandem copy of the complete mitochondrial genome, revealing their monophyletic origin. Moreover, we demonstrate that chromosomal gaps in both sequenced libraries were redundant to each other, indicating selective constraint on their use by M. furry disorder and the incapability of the M. mercurialis sequence to invade a closed gap. Our findings also identify the potential for MFD and M. mercurialis to be used as human therapeutic agents and warrant further exploration of their adaptation to a predominantly microbial environment.

Cribriforms are parasitic endoparasites of protostomes. Most babesia species belong to the genus Babesia, which, due to his genome, are endemic in monogenetic erythrocytosis, a systemic infectious disease that may affect over 1% of the world's population. Here, we determine an eDNA-based multiplex PCR-based integrative molecular phylogeny for a collection of 80 cytomegalovirus (CMV) from 30 different species. Based on our study, we document a new karyotype-independent karyotypic relationship between cytomegalovirus, herpesvirus rpoD, cytomegalovirus I-A/B, and coronavirus type 2 (USCV2). Due to the high rate of evolution of CMV within Babesia, the finding of this karyotypic relationship, when pairing in nature, could have important implications for the diagnosis, diagnosis with sequencing-based assays, and vaccine development. Nevertheless, the M100 cytomegalovirus is still understudied in the context of B. picorna, the primary reservoir for human cytomegalovirus infection. Because of its similarities to CMV, it is highly susceptible to infection by both clinical types of B. picorna, so it is considered a risk factor for human chlamydiosis in endemic areas.

Lyme borreliosis is a tick-borne infectious disease affecting the peripheral blood and severely can affect the cardiovascular system. In turn, cardiovascular damage can lead to fatal outcomes. Therefore, a better understanding of the cardiovascular damage and the identity of the DNA locus of genetic defects involved is of great importance to the assessment of L. minor Spiroplasma infection. In this study, the phylogenetic tree of the Spiroplasma species was constructed for the first time using morphological characteristics and nuclear rDNA sequences. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the Spiroplasma genus has a different diversity from the previously studied Spiroplasma taxa, including a clade with 63 verified strains, one of them has four consecutive type strains. The sequence identity of the reconstructed Spiroplasma minor spirosea species was higher than 98% among all the member of the Spiroplasma genus. Three staphylococcal-like highly conserved region (SCLR) elements were found in the Spiroplasma minor spirosea strain. The overlap of the nematode and the arthropod chitin-binding proteins (CHBPs) from the Spiroplasma minor spirosea strain was quite low and was only found in nematodes and only when single was formed.

Bacteria can survive in highly saline environments, such as the rumen (the mammalian gut where bacteria of the same species play an important role in microbial digestion), and these organisms employ complex, tight co-evolutionary mutualisms, notably those with fungi and insects. Despite the molecular complexity of these symbioses, it remains unclear how the bacteria influence the fungal and insect sexual evolution to contribute to their reproductive success. Using transcriptomic methods, we show that many bacterial species residing in the ruminal enteric microbiome are essential for the complete sexual reproduction of the rumen fungus Trichuris equinus, which, unlike other intestinal pathogens, lacks an externally pathogenic host. Furthermore, we show that these bacteria are rarely just transited through the ruminal microbiota, but transform and maintain lineages linked to a rigid expectation of RNA transfer into the fungal fungus. Our findings identify a molecular mechanism which causes the maintenance of antibiotic resistance, motility, and reproductive success in the fungal fungus Trichuris equinus.

Leishmania braziliensis is a fungal parasite that causes visceral leishmaniasis in south America, including Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Paraguay and Uruguay. It is the only species causing natural infection in humans. The disease is a neglected tropical disease, affecting mainly indigenous communities, having no available treatment. In addition, the infection causes an extensive, continuous and costly re-diagnosis of clinical leishmania infections, which also involve at least 20 pyrogen tests. Some infections can have a latent form. For these infections, a reliable and new diagnosis is very necessary. One way to address this issue would be to measure the COVID-19 spike protein and the immunity induced by the Spike-specific, cytokines-mediated lysis of leishmania. We developed a mathematical model of systemic inflammation and immune response triggered by the immune activation of leishmania, which we named ImmuneComp. We measured the response in a patient who received treatment with amphotericin, a leishmanicidal drug. We built an epidemiological model simulating population vaccination, to explore the relationship between vaccination, period of patient prognosis, duration of treatment, time between the initial focus of the disease and diagnosis and time of the evolution of the form between the two cases.

Candida infections in immunocompromised host are major source of morbidity, but the primary target mycobacterial strain becomes established in man, and typically causes disease. A common mechanism of acquisition is colonization by mobile genetic elements (mGEs) such as plasmids and integrons, carried on the mobile DNA pool, transposons (T) and inverted repeats (IRs), that can be transmitted vertically between generations without being found by the host. In host-associated candidiasis, submicrogram amounts of DNA can be detected in draining peripheral blood. Here we report a rapid approach that can detect Tn and Ir sequences from PCR products of common Candida isolates. In vitro this approach allows for the detection of Tn and Ir sequences in a high level of purity (400 organisms/sample). Here, we apply this method to samples from Burkitt lymphoma patients, confirming Tn and Ir sequences in samples that previously could not be detected by PCR and solid-phase screening. The presence of Tn and Ir sequences in intra-leukemic cells that constitute the Burkitt lymphoma precursor population can be explained by vertical transmission of mGEs from previously healthy cells. Additionally, our results demonstrate that the Tn2D (SDR45/HospR) extrachromosomal plasmid (ecP-SDR45) has transposable elements and mobile genetic elements in its genome and can form integrated host-associated recurrent infections. This study was validated using an integrated diagnostic panel for genital candidiasis from Asian populations and will inform the understanding of mobile genetic elements in the pathogenesis of serious human infections.

Orflogy (or cryptic symbiosis) is a generalist detrimental syndrome associated with alien microbial invaders in natural settings. The scope of this review encompasses various aspects of orflogy: transmission and disease susceptibility, with a focus on a pathogenic oral bacterium, Fusobacterium nucleatum. Specific descriptions are provided for the earliest occurrence, transmission, and transmission dynamics, the interaction with host innate immunity, disease ecology, and treatment strategies. Additionally, this review integrates insights on the global ecological significance of fungal novelties related to under-characterized species and infection pathways, offering perspectives on potential prevention strategies to mitigate orflogy.

Trophozoites, sperm-like microorganisms, serve as a major source of infectious disease through viruses. Despite their critical importance, the mechanisms regulating the acquisition of function in the torpedoed stage, transitioning from parasitic motility to dominant, vascularized, comma-like stages, remains poorly understood. However, it is known that motile stages harbor a conserved flagellum-like structure known as anfE. Here, we profiled six T. gondii amastigotes to elucidate their maturation into aphoptoides. At 28 hours after incubation, aphoptoides exhibited a sudden transition from 400nm filamentous to smooth smooth flagellar morphology, evolving over 18 hours. Importantly, aphoptoides became more readily transmitted to animals, initiating the formation of aphoptoides tumors, which clearly displayed the common amoeboid-like developmental features of transposons. Finally, mutation analysis showed that nucleotide position 7116 repeats 19 amino acids. Remarkably, mutating this region abrogated the ability of aphoptoides to invade mammalian cell lines, suggesting the structure of aphoptoides is critical for avidity and trafficking. Altogether, this study establishes aphoptoides as a physiologically active intermediate during the aculeolate stage from T. gondii infection.

In contrast to the eukaryotic fungal pathogen Candida albicans, almost all gut fungal infections are caused by candi-abaci that usually harbor no pathogenic genes yet exert detrimental effects on host health and growth. Here, we investigate Candida albicans colonization of the microbial cascade controlling the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT). Colonization of human enteric tissues is a highly complex process consisting of complex interactions involving many different bacterial strains and lineages as well as complex molecular pathways including microRNAs. However, the diverse bacteriophages (prophage), retroviruses (prPh) and lisogene (eLin) producing member in the obligate parasite Chytridiomycota are poorly characterised. Indeed, little is known about their contribution to the pathogenesis in vivo. Here we provide detailed insight into the genome architecture of the C. albicans phages and the role of three different virus-host intracellular pathogens, viz. ChoMoF (cryptic obligate obligate intracellular protozoan endosymbiont parasitizing C. albicans), TsMY (chytridiomycota intracellular parasite) and LysLMP-2 (lysogenic intracellular monoorganism inhibiting host cell defence), identified within the community of C. albicans. The complete genomic composition of these three phages was determined from 1000-fold sequenced metagenomic libraries collected from faeces and clinical samples. We used multiple bi-dimensional oligonucleotide affinity electrophoresis (ADA) and capture libraries to characterise their genomes and identify their respective functions. Ultimately, all three parasites accounted for 10-100 times higher contribution in comparative with the non-virulent C. albicans, however they also showed high virulence and environmental stress resistance phenotypes. Notably, all three phages complemented each other, enabling the C. albicans to proliferate from different infectives in the GALT at the same time.
sample_p_texts: Balamuthia mandrillaris is a free-living amoeba that can infect the central nervous system to cause granulomatous amebic encephalitis (GAE), a highly fatal disease with mortality rates up to 90%. GAE is typically treated with a six-drug regimen with limited efficacy and significant toxicity. Our lab previously identified nitroxoline, a quinolone antibiotic, as a promising therapeutic complement to the existing regimen, and in 2021 nitroxoline was first successfully used to treat a human patient. In this study, we elucidate nitroxolines mechanism of action using a combination of genomics, transcriptomics, chemical complementation, growth assays, and electron microscopy. In service of this goal, an annotated draft genome of B. mandrillaris strain CDC:V039 was generated using long read sequencing, yielding 88 telomere-to-telomere contigs and over 25,000 protein coding genes. Leveraging this resource, comparative transcriptomics were used to characterize encystment responses to three different cellular stressors: nitroxoline, galactose, and hypoxia. Our findings reveal that nitroxoline-induced cysts undergo transcriptional collapse and genomic and structural destabilization via copper and iron chelation. These data provide insight into nitroxolines multifaceted impact on B. mandrillaris growth and cellular processes and advance our understanding of the transcriptional landscape associated with stress induced encystment. Our findings support the continued clinical study of nitroxoline.

The phylum Chlamydiota consists of obligate intracellular bacteria comprising the human pathogen Chlamydia trachomatis and a large variety of species infecting animals and protists. Despite their enormous diversity, a feature shared by all known chlamydiae is their biphasic developmental cycle, consisting of intra- and extracellular stages with substantial differences in morphology and physiology. A similarly remarkable shift occurs in the amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum and related dictyostelids in their so-called social life cycle, leading to the formation of spores through aggregation of vegetative trophozoites and the development of multicellular fruiting bodies. Although dictyostelids undergo symbioses with various bacteria, chlamydiae have only recently been found to be associated with this host. Here we report the isolation of a Dictyostelium giganteum strain naturally infected with a chlamydial symbiont, identified as a novel species, Reclusachlamydia socialis. The symbiont is retained in all stages of the hosts social life cycle and notably lacks an extracellular form. Combining fluorescence microscopy and quantitative PCR we showed that transmission is entirely dependent on cell-to-cell contact during the host aggregation stage. The absence of an extracellular stage is further supported by transmission electron microscopy and the lack of genes essential for chlamydial developmental cycle regulation and extracellular survival. This unprecedented variation of a highly conserved developmental feature that evolved more than a billion years ago illustrates the remarkable adaptability of chlamydiae. This study adds to our understanding of endosymbiosis in the face of facultative multicellularity.

Influenza A virus (IAV) causes annual morbidity and mortality and remains a constant pandemic threat due to emergence of novel strains. Therefore, understanding the factors important in host-to-host transmission of IAV is a key control point for protecting individual and public health. Transmission is highly heterogeneous with viral factors and host inflammatory and immune factors being implicated. Also implicated is the upper respiratory microbiome. While typically thought to act indirectly on viral pathogenesis, in an immunomodulatory capacity to enhance or reduce susceptibility to viral infection, recent studies on the pathogenesis of IAV have identified direct interactions between the virus and upper respiratory pathobiont bacteria. We hypothesize that the bacterial cells and their metabolites co-shed into respiratory droplets with IAV particles, can alter the viability of the IAV particles in the environment, and therefore altering the capacity for host-to-host transmission. In this investigation we utilize a simplified model of fomite transmission in the absence of confounding host factors and demonstrate how oxidative stress from both the environment and the metabolic activity of S. pneumoniae contribute to the killing of IAV, while catalase or the metabolic activity of S. aureus can protect IAV from environmental or pneumococcally-produced reactive oxygen species.

Giardia duodenalis is a binuclear protozoan that causes intestinal infection in humans and animals. The life cycle of G. duodenalis is comprised by 2 stages: trophozoite (vegetative, ploidy: 4N) and cyst (infective, ploidy: 8-16N) and the transition from one to another requires a precise coordination as well as the support of the DNA repair machinery. While DNA homologous recombination DNA repair has recently been characterized, NER and BER are pathways that had not been explored. Most of the structure specific enzymes (SSE) participate in a variety of processes like DNA replication stress, DNA adduct repair, Holliday junction processing. In an effort to explore these kinds of enzymes in G. duodenalis, a minimalist parasite, we aimed at characterizing the Fen1 enzyme by cloning its gene to study its catalytic properties (binding and nuclease) using flap and bubble DNA substrates. Unexpectedly, we found that GdFen-1 is able to cleave bubble DNA, then to shed light on which domains of this enzyme are responsible for this activity, giardial acid block and a portion of a cap region were substituted by their human counterparts, and while acid block substitution did not affect this activity, the modification in the cap region did. The possible implications of these findings are addressed.

Trypanosoma cruzi possesses hundreds of genes associated with its pathogenesis. The extent and organization of this diverse gene repertoire, expression, and role in infection remain unclear. Using accurate long-read sequencing and chromatin conformation capture, T. cruzi chromosomes were assembled from telomere-to-telomere. The genome revealed multigene families of virulence genes accounting for [~]70% of some chromosomes, organized in clusters or scattered through housekeeping genes. Quantitative proteomics identified stage-specific proteins and numerous trans-sialidases upregulated in trypomastigotes. Notably, the expression of virulence gene families changed stochastically in trypomastigotes, conferring T. cruzi fitness to cardiomyocyte infection while diversifying the invasion to multiple tissues. A T. cruzi genome-wide yeast surface display screen against Chagas disease patients antibodies revealed virulence genes expressed during human infections. However, limited conservation in their antibody-binding sites suggests their sequence diversity and variation help parasites avert antibody recognition. The data point to a role for virulence multigene families in infection persistence.

sample_q_texts: Understanding the impact of neurobiological factors in neurodegenerative and non-neurodegenerative cancers is crucial for medical professionals to develop early diagnosis, prognostics and treatments. Recently, we developed a voxel-based imaging MR based estimation of tumour neurobiological functional changes using ultra-low-dose whole-brain linear acquisition. We explored this unique dataset by developing a voxel-based neurocognitive (Neuro)QoL modelling framework to unravel the impact of tumours on neurocognitive functions. The validated two-layer NeuroQoL model considers neuroimaging and neurocognitive data, which provides discrimination between patients with or without cognitive impairment. We established that the NeuroQoL model accurately classifies patients with tumour-based cognitive impairment (CBSI), allowing for timely screening and making the distinction between patients with and without CBSI. Notably, this model was shown to be robust to up to 5.2 degrees in lesion count. Remarkably, the predicted NeuroQoL scores account for cortical demyelination with no changes in resting T1 and N1 signals. This framework could enable future studies to understand the underlying mechanism of neurocognitive changes related to neurobiological alterations in various neurodegenerative and non-neurodegenerative cancer, also including head and neck cancer.

To characterize how aging affects hippocampal and paralimbic networks, we studied brain networks based on 145 healthy human adult brains undergoing magnetic resonance imaging in the Healthy Aging Study. These healthy individuals had significant age-related volume declines in anterior medial temporal regions typical of aging populations, particularly within parietal neocortical and hippocampus structures. We conducted a t-test to rank volunteers in the three main age groups; 30 years, 40 years and 50 years. Our results showed that each three-age group had age-related changes, but differences across age groups were greatest in the parietal cortex and hippocampus. Notably, our results indicate that while differences across groups were more pronounced in the hippocampus (e.g., spatial memory, memory consolidation and episodic retrieval, inhibitory control, working memory, visuospatial processing) than in the parietal cortex (memory consolidation, cognitive control, working memory, and sequential processing), differences were present across these brain regions as well as in all of the networks studied. To further assess the significance of these differences, we compared age-related network differences among 30-year-olds, 40-year-olds and 50-year-olds and detected differences by comparing networks among those six age groups to those of younger volunteers (aged between 26 and 31 years). For 40-year-olds, although still relatively young and healthy, our results suggest differences in temporal association network between hippocampal and parahippocampal regions, which is consistent with previous observations. These findings provide insights into the patterns of age-related brain changes in frontal and temporal human medial temporal regions and its implications for cognitive function.

Women-specific data provides insights into neurodegenerative diseases, but studies using middle-aged and elderly women as the primary subjects may require amendment to generate reliable male-friendly datasets for aging mechanisms and disease-modifying approaches. Here we demonstrate the utility of the adult male brain as a resource for neuro-friendly modeling of sex-specific aging brain networks. We conducted voxel-based morphometric (VBM) analysis of 362 adult middle-aged to older male brains to investigate sex differences in cortical gray matter (GM) volumes, motor unit size, myelination, and microglia. We examined bilateral structures, which are regions consistently reduced with age in male brains but present relative preservation in female brains. Results show robust gender differences in sexual dimorphism among age-matched brains, supporting the consistency of male aging and disruption of the human white-matter and myelin systems. Further, we found that adult males retain key sex-specific myelin age and volume changes, including a decrease in the number of axons in the white matter substantia nigra. This contrasts with female brains, showing a similar increase in the number of neurons (related to the growth of axons) within the substantia nigra but a decrease in long-range cytoarchitectural complexity across regions. Overall, these results demonstrate that gender-disaggregated datasets are informative tools for better understanding sex-specific and disease-specific brain dynamics.

Significance statementGrowing evidence from multi-omics-based aging studies suggests that sex-disaggregated data may provide meaningful insights in navigating biological aging, particularly in advancing our understanding of sex-specific neurological and neurodegenerative differences. However, integrating sex-disaggregated data challenges the need to acculturate data to a more restricted human-only database; the male-specific human brain atlas and cognitive profiles have a severe disadvantage in comparability across other human traits. In line with this, the traditional male-specific and female-specific mammalian brain atlas models only differ by a few dozen neurons across a large variety of mammals, resulting in significant difficulties in disentangling neural mechanisms that shape sex-specific brain activity. This paper demonstrates the utility of the mammalian human brain atlas in generating a cross-species, sex-neutral human male-specific model, which has the advantage of allowing additional hardware/data layering for disease modeling and comparison. With this tool, we show that sex-disaggregated data analysis of existing male-specific databases provides the most robust method for investigating the brain of males to inform future studies of sex-specific, age-associated alterations to the gray and white matter,

IntroductionCerebral plaque volume predicts clinical severity and mortality in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD). The beta-amyloid peptide (Abeta) plaque volume of the left parietal cortex, normally contained within a spherical punctate structure, is quantified at the cortical surface in the X2 planes using software PACS 3D rendering. There is currently no standard for quantification of intracortical beta-amyloid plaques in AD patients.ResultsWe quantified at-a-time PSMA and D72VL lambda (D72VL lambda) beta-amyloid plaque volumes in 262 AD patients and compared these with traditional estimates. Measures of beta-amyloid plaque complexity included the Bland-Altman statistic and the Bland-Altman core regions for conventional and spherical geometric size in the cortical layer I or II.D72VL lambda beta-amyloid plaque volume measures were superior to conventional beta-amyloid plaque volume measures in detecting patients with beta-amyloid plaque. Importantly, the Bland-Altman core region estimator (BCM-23) was able to detect patients with beta-amyloid plaque volume between 0.82 and 1.86. BCM-23 also discriminated plaques which differed from typically arranged cortical plaques.Bland-Altman core region and BCM-23 were shown to discriminate beta-amyloid plaque volume between -0.74 and -0.42, from the mean of this class, with adequate precision to identify clinically significant beta-amyloid plaque volume distributions. Accordingly, in the clinical trial of an investigator-initiated augmentation therapy in young AD patients the BCM-23 threshold discriminated patients with low, medium, and high beta-amyloid plaque volumes.CONCLUSIONThe BCM-23 algorithm may serve as a standard for quantifying beta-amyloid plaque volume in AD patients, whilst Bland-Altman core region is an alternative to this algorithm.

Brain volume is a dynamic metric that alters following infancy and early adulthood, and it serves as a vital biomarker for understanding the brain, maturing relationships, and the manifestation of mental disorders. Though brain MRI has become a mainstay for diagnosing neurological disorders, cell-size measurement by neuroimaging still remains a scarce option for clinicians. Here, we report on a cell-size analysis approach based on time-resolved fluorescence measurements of cryopreserved brain slices. This approach can be customized to yield information on several brain regions such as the prefrontal cortex, hippocampal dentate gyrus, hippocampal CA1 region, entorhinal cortex, hippocampus cornu ammonis, primary motor cortex, and layers of subventricular zone of the hippocampus. Such assessment is particularly valuable for individuals with early onset cognitive impairment, large volumes of testicles, or no identifiable imaging results in MRI, thus identifying separate sub-populations of individuals on the basis of volume-dependent cortical molecular biomarkers.

BACKGROUNDWhite matter atrophy (WMA) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is typically diagnosed in the temporal lobes based on structural magnetic resonance imaging. New MRI techniques offer the potential to detect WMA in deeper structures, at least partly due to a growing appreciation that cortical connectivity also changes with aging.

RESEARCH QUESTIONDo connectivity alterations linked to neural loss or neurodegeneration contribute to differential trends in WMA between older and younger age groups?

METHODSFirst, we investigated relationships between functional measures that distinguish AD and other related conditions such as other dementias, probable cognitive impairment, and amnestic mild cognitive impairment.

RESULTSMeasurement of regional cerebral blood flow to frontal and insula cortices revealed significant differences between older and younger age groups. Predictive modeling revealed the potential utility of DTI tractography and functional connectivity measures to distinguish AD from neurodegenerative conditions with low risk for Alzheimer's dementia.

IMPLICATIONSOur findings indicate that white matter atrophy and other tissue-level hallmarks of WMA may contribute to differential changes in functional connectivity in prefrontal and medial temporal lobes during aging.
sample_p_texts: Accumulation of abnormal tau protein into neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) is a pathologic hallmark of Alzheimer disease (AD). Accurate detection of NFTs in tissue samples can reveal relationships with clinical, demographic, and genetic features through deep phenotyping. However, expert manual analysis is time-consuming, subject to observer variability, and cannot handle the data amounts generated by modern imaging. We present a scalable, open-source, deep-learning approach to quantify NFT burden in digital whole slide images (WSIs) of post-mortem human brain tissue. To achieve this, we developed a method to generate detailed NFT boundaries directly from single-point-per-NFT annotations. We then trained a semantic segmentation model on 45 annotated 2400{micro}m by 1200{micro}m regions of interest (ROIs) selected from 15 unique temporal cortex WSIs of AD cases from three institutions (University of California (UC)-Davis, UC-San Diego, and Columbia University). Segmenting NFTs at the single-pixel level, the model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic of 0.832 and an F1 of 0.527 (196-fold over random) on a held-out test set of 664 NFTs from 20 ROIs (7 WSIs). We compared this to deep object detection, which achieved comparable but coarser-grained performance that was 60% faster. The segmentation and object detection models correlated well with expert semi-quantitative scores at the whole-slide level (Spearmans rho {rho}=0.654 (p=6.50e-5) and {rho}=0.513 (p=3.18e-3), respectively). We openly release this multi-institution deep-learning pipeline to provide detailed NFT spatial distribution and morphology analysis capability at a scale otherwise infeasible by manual assessment.

Predicting cognitive decline using MRI measures of brain volume is challenging. Normative models capture the evolution of biomarkers over time in a healthy group, quantifying an individuals deviation from that norm. Here, we improve the precision of normative models for hippocampal volume, a key cognitive biomarker, by integrating multi-threshold polygenic scores (PGS) that capture genetic predisposition to its variability. We built Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) models on genetic, imaging, and demographic data from 23,997 UK Biobank (UKBB) participants, validating on 3,000 out-of-sample participants from the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and the European Prevention of Alzheimers Disease (EPAD) cohorts. The genetically-informed models improved associations significantly across five experimental designs and 13 key neurocognitive measures, including Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), Alzheimers Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS), and importantly, improving prediction of future cognitive decline. These findings underscore the value of integrating multi-threshold PGS with neuroimaging-based predictive models for improving prognostication in neurodegenerative diseases.

Differences in the volumes of brain structures between individuals are often linked to various conditions, including Alzheimers disease, schizophrenia, and overall brain health. However, it remains unclear to what extent these differences reflect individual levels present at young adulthood or diverging aging trajectories at later ages. In this study, we analyze the aging dynamics of the volume of six brain structures based on MRI scans from a large cross-cohort longitudinal sample of cognitively healthy adults (n = 8,311 with 18,520 MRIs, ages from 18 to 97 years). From general assumptions about structural brain dynamics and measurement noise, a stochastic dynamical model was fit to the data to estimate both the variability and persistence of structural changes across adulthood. Using this model, we calculated how much of the variance in individual volumetric differences can be attributed to stable levels from young adulthood versus systematic changes at older ages, as well as the theoretical sensitivity of longitudinal studies to detect individual differences in changes. The findings were as follows: 1) Before age 60 years, inter-individual differences in neuroanatomical volumes almost exclusively reflect stable differences between individuals, while the influence from systematic differences in rate-of-change increases thereafter; up to 40 % of the variation being due to differences in change at 80 years. In contrast, ventricular volume reflects differences in change from early adulthood. 2) Current brain age-models are unlikely to be sensitive to detect differences in aging trajectories. 3) Imaging studies have a low reliability to detect inter-individual brain change before age 60. After 60 years, the study reliability increases sharply with longer intervals between scans and more modestly with additional intermediate observations. In conclusion, it is critical to distinguish stable levels from early adulthood from systematic differences in change when studying adult brain aging.

Research on structural networks often suffers from limited sample sizes and inherent selection biases in individual studies, which restrict their ability to address complex questions regarding human brain organization. Pooling data across studies is crucial for achieving a more comprehensive representation of the population and effectively managing individual heterogeneity; however, structural networks acquired from multiple sites are susceptible to significant site-related differences. This necessitates harmonization to mitigate biases and reveal true biological variability in multi-site analyses. Our work marks the first effort to develop and evaluate harmonization frameworks specifically for structural networks. We adapt several statistical approaches for harmonizing structural networks and provide a comprehensive evaluation to rigorously test their effectiveness. Our findings demonstrate that the adaptation of the Gamma Generalized Linear Model (gamma-GLM) outperforms other methods in modeling structural network data, effectively eliminating site-related effects in structural connectivity matrices and downstream graph-based analyses while preserving biological variability. Additionally, we highlight gamma-GLMs superiority in addressing confounding factors between site and age. Two practical applications further illustrate the utility of our harmonization framework in tackling common challenges in multi-site structural network studies. Specifically, harmonization using gamma-GLM enhances the transferability of brain age predictors to new datasets and facilitates data integration in patient studies, ultimately improving statistical power. Together, our work offers essential guidelines for harmonizing and integrating multi-site structural network studies, paving the way for more robust discoveries through collaborative research in the era of big data.

The concept of brain age (BA) describes an integrative imaging marker of brain health, often suggested to reflect ageing processes. However, the degree to which cross-sectional MRI features, including BA, reflect past, ongoing and future brain changes across different tissue types from macro-to microstructure remains controversial (Vidal-Pineiro et al. 2021). Here, we advance these findings by using multimodal imaging data of 39, 325 UK Biobank participants, aged 44 - 82 years at baseline and 2, 520 follow-ups within 1.12 - 6.90 years. In concordance with the original findings, we find insufficient evidence that BA reflects the rate of brain ageing. However, modality-specific differences in brain ages reflected the state of the brain, highlighting diffusion and multimodal MRI brain age as potentially useful cross-sectional markers.

The world population is shifting sharply toward an older-age demographic. To navigate the escalating burden of physical and cognitive decline common to aging, and heightened risk of neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disease, we require advances in treatment and prevention interventions. These advances are predicated on attaining a deeper understanding of the molecular processes underlying brain aging. Here, we employed novel GWAS and cis-eQTL-based polygenic risk scores (GWASAGE-PRS and cis-eQTLAGE-PRS) indexing genetic risk for accelerated molecular brain aging, and examined their associations with cortical thickness and performance in age-sensitive cognitive domains in 31 384 participants (16 392 women, age 64.1{+/-}7.65) from the UK Biobank. While GWASAGE-PRS was nominally associated with lower cortical thickness in frontotemporal regions, cis-eQTLAGE-PRS displayed robust associations with greater cortical thickness in age-sensitive frontal, temporal, and parietal regions, including the left and right precentral (pFDR<0.0001, pFDR=0.05), left insula (pFDR=0.05), as well as the right supramarginal (pFDR=0.05) and precuneus (pFDR=0.05) regions. Similar pFDR trending associations occurred bilaterally in the caudal middle frontal (pFDR=0.052, pFDR=0.078) and right insula (pFDR=0.071). These structural findings co-occurred alongside increased executive function performance on the Trail Making Test B (pFDR=0.035), suggesting a potential neurostructural and cognitive reserve phenotype. This resilience profile may reflect previously uncharacterized pathways of brain reserve in age-related pathology, informing future translational research identifying novel treatment and prevention targets.

INTRODUCTIONLike gray matter (GM), white matter (WM) BOLD functional signals change in preclinical AD. However, the potential of WM BOLD for identifying preclinical AD remains underexplored.

METHODSWe developed BrainVAE, a transformer-based variational autoencoder with interpretability, to classify preclinical AD and normal controls using resting-state fMRI data. We benchmarked BrainVAE against nine alternative models under three input configurations: WM-only, GM-only, and combined WM+GM. Interpretability analysis was also performed to investigate each brain regions contribution to the classification task.

RESULTSBrainVAE outperformed other models and performed well (accuracy = 83.42%, F1-score = 91.62%, AUC = 64.50%) using the combined input compared to WM-only and GM-only. Specific WM bundles--including corpus callosum, fornix, and corticospinal tract--were among the most influential features contributing to the classification.

DISCUSSIONIncorporating WM BOLD signals improves the distinction of preclinical AD from controls, underscoring the potential role of WM BOLD features for detecting early-stage AD.
